translation_en:
Yang Fu, courtesy name Zhenqing, was registered in Xichong County, Shunqing Prefecture, Sichuan, in a military household. A county school student specializing in the Book of Changes, he ranked first among his brothers and was aged twenty-five, born on the fourteenth day of the intercalary eighth month. His great-grandfather was Chun, a Clerk; his grandfather was Ru; and his father was Linghan. His mother was née Ren. Both parents were living. His younger brother was Min, and his wife was née Luo. He placed fourteenth in the Sichuan Provincial Examination and 285th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Li Tinggui, courtesy name Zixin, was registered in Changzhi County, Lu’an Prefecture, Shanxi, in a military household. A student of the Directorate of Education specializing in the Book of Changes, he ranked first among his brothers and was aged forty-two, born on the tenth day of the sixth month. His great-grandfather was Yu, an Office Assistant in the Court of Imperial Entertainments, posthumously granted the title Gentleman for Service (zhengshi lang); his grandfather was Tan, an honorary Official for Longevity; and his father was Hao, a Vice Prefect. His legal mother was née Cui, his stepmother née Zhang, and his birth mother née Yang. Both parents were deceased. His elder brothers were Chongshi, Chonggeng, and Chongli (充𥟖); his younger brothers were Chongmei, a tribute scholar; Tingzhang, a Ceremonial Escort; Chongdao, Chongbing, Chongdong, Chonghui, Chongfu, and Chongrong. His wife was née Wang. He placed sixtieth in the Shanxi Provincial Examination and 288th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Chen Can, courtesy name Derun, was registered in Baling County, Yuezhou Prefecture, Huguang, in a military household. A student of the Directorate of Education specializing in the Book of Odes, he ranked first among his brothers and was aged thirty, born on the fifth day of the first month. His great-grandfather was Pu; his grandfather was Bosheng; and his father was Shunmo, a Sacrificial Attendant. His mother was née Zhang, and his stepmother née Tan. Both parents were living. His younger brothers were Ai, Mei, Yan, Xiang, Jie, and Yu. His wife was née Liu; he subsequently became betrothed to a woman née Chai. He placed thirty-fourth in the Huguang Provincial Examination and ninetieth in the Metropolitan Examination.

Chen Xiaogu, courtesy name Wuzhou, was registered in Xi County, Guang Subprefecture, Runing Prefecture, Henan, in a civilian household. A student of the Directorate of Education specializing in the Book of Changes, he ranked second among his brothers and was aged forty, born on the fourteenth day of the eighth month. His great-grandfather was Rang; his grandfather was Hai; and his father was Ziqian, an Assistant Instructor. His mother was née Chen. Both parents were deceased. His elder brother was Mugu, and his younger brother was Yungu. His wife was née Lei. He placed fiftieth in the Henan Provincial Examination and 259th in the Metropolitan Examination.

邵稷〔貫浙江紹興府餘姚縣民籍，縣學附學生，治易經，字子嘉，行二，年三十二，十月初六日生〕。曾祖禮〔知縣〕，祖孟甫〔中書舍人〕，父至，母胡氏。具慶下，兄濤，弟漳〔同科進士〕、沺、淠、晙、涷、漣、瀍、澮。娶胡氏，繼娶姜氏。浙江鄉試第二十九名，會試第七名。

楊允繩〔貫直隸松江府華亭縣匠籍，國子生，治詩經，字翼少，行一，年三十五，十月初三日生〕。曾祖雲〔贈承德郎、工部主事〕，祖瑋〔四川按察司副使〕，父秉道，母戴氏。永感下，娶黃氏。順天府鄉試第六十二名，會試第一百七十二名。

趙輄〔貫山西澤州高平縣民籍，國子生，治易經，字以載，行二，年三十六，六月十六日生〕。曾祖子成〔義官〕，祖倫〔義官〕，父科〔農官〕，母秦氏，繼母范氏。具慶下，兄軸，弟金〔監生〕、麟。娶李氏。山西鄉試第十一名，會試第五十名。
translation_en:
Wan Shan, registered in an official household of the Dingliao Front Guard under the Liaodong Regional Military Commission, was a native of Linchuan County, Fuzhou Prefecture, Jiangxi. An Imperial University student specializing in the Book of Documents, he had the courtesy name Yizhi and was second in birth order, aged forty, born on the fourth day of the ninth lunar month. His great-grandfather Jun, grandfather Ying, and father Yue were all Company Commanders; his mother was née Wang. Both parents were living. His elder brother Tang was a Company Commander, and his younger brothers were Yan and Xi. He married a woman née Liu and subsequently women née Chen and Sun. He placed seventy-seventh in the Shuntian Prefecture Provincial Examination and 203rd in the Metropolitan Examination.

Shao Ji was registered in a civilian household in Yuyao County, Shaoxing Prefecture, Zhejiang. An attached student of the county school specializing in the Book of Changes, he had the courtesy name Zijia and was second in birth order, aged thirty-two, born on the sixth day of the tenth lunar month. His great-grandfather Li was a District Magistrate, his grandfather Mengfu a Secretariat Drafter, his father Zhi, and his mother née Hu. Both parents were living. His elder brother was Tao; his younger brothers were Zhang, a jinshi of the same examination cohort, Tian, Pi, Jun, Dong, Lian, Chan, and Hui. He married a woman née Hu and subsequently a woman née Jiang. He placed twenty-ninth in the Zhejiang Provincial Examination and seventh in the Metropolitan Examination.

Yang Yunsheng was registered in an artisan household in Huating County, Songjiang Prefecture, in the directly administered metropolitan region. An Imperial University student specializing in the Book of Odes, he had the courtesy name Yishao and was first in birth order, aged thirty-five, born on the third day of the tenth lunar month. His great-grandfather Yun was posthumously granted the titles Gentleman for Fulfillment of Virtue and Bureau Secretary in the Ministry of Works; his grandfather Wei was Vice Commissioner of the Sichuan Provincial Surveillance Commission. His father was Bingdao and his mother née Dai. Both parents were deceased. He married a woman née Huang. He placed sixty-second in the Shuntian Prefecture Provincial Examination and 172nd in the Metropolitan Examination.

Zhao Guang was registered in a civilian household in Gaoping County, Zezhou, Shanxi. An Imperial University student specializing in the Book of Changes, he had the courtesy name Yizai and was second in birth order, aged thirty-six, born on the sixteenth day of the sixth lunar month. His great-grandfather Zicheng and grandfather Lun each held the honorary title Official for Righteousness; his father Ke was an Agricultural Official. His mother was née Qin and his stepmother née Fan. Both parents were living. His elder brother was Zhou; his younger brothers were Jin, an Imperial University student, and Lin. He married a woman née Li. He placed eleventh in the Shanxi Provincial Examination and fiftieth in the Metropolitan Examination.

translation_en:
Cao Fu 曹鈇, courtesy name Youwen, was registered in a civilian household in Qu County, Shunqing Prefecture, Sichuan. A county school student specializing in the Book of Rites, he ranked second among his brothers and was thirty sui old, born on the second day of the eleventh lunar month. His great-grandfather was Yanbin, his grandfather You, and his father Mengzan; his father's former wife was née Chen, his mother née Wu, and his stepmother née Mao. Both parents were deceased. His elder brother was Yue and his younger brother Qi; his wife was née Cai. He placed twenty-first in the Sichuan Provincial Examination and 192nd in the Metropolitan Examination.

Shen Zhong 申仲, courtesy name Cimeng, was registered in a military household in Renqiu County, Hejian Prefecture, and was a native of Tunliu County, Lu'an Prefecture, Shanxi. A county school student specializing in the Book of Odes, he ranked fourth among his brothers and was thirty-five sui old, born on the nineteenth day of the twelfth lunar month. His great-grandfather Qing was a Commissioner; his grandfather was Ying, his father Xu, and his mother née Gao. Both parents were living. His elder brothers were You, Xin, and Wei, and his younger brothers Xiu and Jie; his wife was née Pang. He placed eighty-third in the Shuntian Prefecture Provincial Examination and 109th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Zhang Tinghuai 張廷槐, courtesy name Zizheng, was registered in an official household of the Xinghe Guard Battalion under the Wanquan Regional Military Commission and was a native of Ji Subprefecture, Shuntian Prefecture. A student of the Imperial University specializing in the Book of Odes, he ranked sixth among his brothers and was thirty-six sui old, born on the twenty-first day of the ninth lunar month. His great-grandfather Xin was a Battalion Commander; his grandfather Jian was posthumously granted the titles of Gentleman for Attendance and Investigating Censor. His father Lian was an Assistant Surveillance Commissioner in Shanxi and formerly an Investigating Censor. His father's former wife, née Ye, was posthumously granted the title of Lady, and his mother, née Ru, was granted the title of Lady. His father was living and his mother deceased. His elder brothers were Jin, a Battalion Commander, Xuan, Tingxiang, Tingdong, and Tingji; his younger brothers were Tinggui, Tingsong, Tingbai, and Tingchun. His wife was née Liu. He placed thirty-eighth in the Shuntian Prefecture Provincial Examination and eighty-third in the Metropolitan Examination.

He Zhang 何璋, courtesy name Guozhen, was registered in a military household in Yiling Subprefecture, Jingzhou Prefecture, Huguang. A student of the Imperial University specializing in the Spring and Autumn Annals, he ranked third among his brothers and was thirty-nine sui old, born on the fifth day of the first lunar month. His great-grandfather was Zong, his grandfather Yu, his father Yongfu, his mother née Deng, and his stepmother née Wang. His father was living and his mother deceased. His elder brothers were Zan, Qi, a County Magistrate, 𤣱 (reading uncertain [?]), and Yao. His wife was née Zhang. He placed fortieth in the Huguang Provincial Examination and seventy-seventh in the Metropolitan Examination.

具慶下 兄瓏 弟環 娶田氏

陳全之〔貫福建福州府閩縣，民籍，縣學附學生，治春秋，字粹中，行三，年三十三，二月十六日生〕。曾祖叔剛〔翰林院侍讀〕，祖煒〔布政使司左布政使〕，父璽，嫡母姚氏，繼母鄧氏，生母王氏。慈侍下，兄壆之、覲之、成之，弟啓之〔陰陽官〕、慎之、朝鍪、約之、寀之、熙之、朝鑨，娶林氏。福建鄉試第二十三名，會試第二百二十二名。

李燧〔貫山東兖州府金鄉縣，軍籍，縣學生，治詩經，字晦夫，行一，年三十，八月初一日生〕。曾祖綱，祖淮〔貢士，贈户部員外郎〕，父楘〔行太僕寺少卿〕，母周氏〔封宜人〕。重慶下，弟炎、燮、燚、燃，娶高氏。山東鄉試第四十二名，會試第二百四十名。

戴才〔貫直隸河間府滄州，民籍，州學生，治詩經，字大需，行一，年二十九，十月十三日生〕。曾祖慶，祖宣，父臣，母蕭氏。具慶下，兄瓏，弟璟，娶田氏。順天府鄉試第五十六名，會試第一百四十五名。
translation_en:
Jin Hao, registered in Lanxi County, Jinhua Prefecture, Zhejiang, belonged to a civilian household and was an added-quota student of the county school. He specialized in the Book of Changes; his courtesy name was Wenxing, and he ranked thirty-fourth in family order. He was thirty-five years old, born on the ninth day of the fifth month. His great-grandfather was Yanliang, his grandfather Shikai, his father Jiao, and his mother née Zhang. Both parents were deceased. His elder brother was Fu, and his younger brothers were Jun and Jie. His wife was née Wang. He placed fifty-eighth in the Zhejiang Provincial Examination and 209th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Chen Quanzhi, registered in Min County, Fuzhou Prefecture, Fujian, belonged to a civilian household and was an attached student of the county school. He specialized in the Spring and Autumn Annals; his courtesy name was Cuizhong, and he ranked third in family order. He was thirty-three years old, born on the sixteenth day of the second month. His great-grandfather was Shugang, Reader in the Hanlin Academy; his grandfather was Wei, Left Provincial Administration Commissioner; and his father was Xi. His father's principal wife was née Yao, his stepmother née Deng, and his birth mother née Wang. His father was deceased, and his mother was living. His elder brothers were Xuezhi, Jinzhi, and Chengzhi; his younger brothers were Qizhi, an official of the Yin-Yang School, Shenzhi, Chaomou, Yuezhi, Caizhi, Xizhi, and Chaolong. His wife was née Lin. He placed twenty-third in the Fujian Provincial Examination and 222nd in the Metropolitan Examination.

Li Sui, registered in Jinxiang County, Yanzhou Prefecture, Shandong, belonged to a military household and was a student of the county school. He specialized in the Book of Odes; his courtesy name was Huifu, and he ranked first in family order. He was thirty years old, born on the first day of the eighth month. His great-grandfather was Gang; his grandfather was Huai, a tribute scholar posthumously appointed Vice Director in the Ministry of Revenue; and his father was Mu, Vice Minister of the Branch Court of the Imperial Stud. His mother, née Zhou, had been granted the title Lady of Suitability. His parents and grandparents were living. His younger brothers were Yan, Xie, Yi, and Ran. His wife was née Gao. He placed forty-second in the Shandong Provincial Examination and 240th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Dai Cai, registered in Cangzhou, Hejian Prefecture, in the directly administered metropolitan region, belonged to a civilian household and was a student of the subprefectural school. He specialized in the Book of Odes; his courtesy name was Daxu, and he ranked first in family order. He was twenty-nine years old, born on the thirteenth day of the tenth month. His great-grandfather was Qing, his grandfather Xuan, his father Chen, and his mother née Xiao. Both parents were living. His elder brother was Long, and his younger brother Jing. His wife was née Tian. He placed fifty-sixth in the Shuntian Prefecture Provincial Examination and 145th in the Metropolitan Examination.

王宗聖〔貫浙江金華府義烏縣民籍，國子生，治書經，字汝學，行五十三，年三十三，六月初七日生〕。曾祖深，祖佺，父敏〔教授〕，母陳氏。嚴侍下，弟宗祖，娶劉氏。浙江鄉試第二十八名，會試第二十一名。

李攀龍〔貫山東濟南府歷城縣民籍，府學生，治詩經，字于鱗，行三，年三十一，四月十八日生〕。曾祖禎，祖端〔義官〕，父寶〔典膳〕，前母郭氏，母張氏。慈侍下，兄登龍、躍龍，弟化龍、成龍，娶徐氏。山東鄉試第二名，會試第三十九名。

范充濁〔貫順天府霸州民籍，國子生，治書經，字清夫，行一，年二十五，九月二十二日生〕。曾祖延壽〔巡檢〕，祖昭，父魁〔歲貢生〕，母王氏。重慶下，弟充愚、充鈍，娶曹氏。順天府鄉試第八十二名，會試第二百七十八名。
translation_en:
Li Fengshi, courtesy name Huafu, was registered in a military household of Dezhou Guard in the directly administered region and was originally from Gan County, Jiangxi. A student of the subprefectural school specializing in the Spring and Autumn Annals, he ranked first in family order, was aged thirty-two, and was born on the tenth day of the tenth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Li Qing; his grandfather, Li Lin; and his father, Li Jie, an honorary official for righteousness. His mother was née Dong. His mother was living and his father deceased. He married a woman née Mao. He placed fifty-fifth in the Shandong Provincial Examination and two hundredth in the Metropolitan Examination.

Wang Zongsheng, courtesy name Ruxue, was registered in a civilian household in Yiwu County, Jinhua Prefecture, Zhejiang. A student of the Directorate of Education specializing in the Book of Documents, he ranked fifty-third in family order, was aged thirty-three, and was born on the seventh day of the sixth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Wang Shen; his grandfather, Wang Quan; and his father, Wang Min, a Prefectural School Instructor. His mother was née Chen. His father was living and his mother deceased. His younger brother was Zongzu. He married a woman née Liu. He placed twenty-eighth in the Zhejiang Provincial Examination and twenty-first in the Metropolitan Examination.

Li Panlong, courtesy name Yulin, was registered in a civilian household in Licheng County, Jinan Prefecture, Shandong. A student of the prefectural school specializing in the Book of Odes, he ranked third in family order, was aged thirty-one, and was born on the eighteenth day of the fourth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Li Zhen; his grandfather, Li Duan, an honorary official for righteousness; and his father, Li Bao, a Steward (dianshan). His father's former wife was née Guo, and his mother was née Zhang. His mother was living and his father deceased. His elder brothers were Denglong and Yuelong; his younger brothers were Hualong and Chenglong. He married a woman née Xu. He placed second in the Shandong Provincial Examination and thirty-ninth in the Metropolitan Examination.

Fan Chongzhuo, courtesy name Qingfu, was registered in a civilian household in Bazhou, Shuntian Prefecture. A student of the Directorate of Education specializing in the Book of Documents, he ranked first in family order, was aged twenty-five, and was born on the twenty-second day of the ninth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Fan Yanshou, a Police Chief; his grandfather, Fan Zhao; and his father, Fan Kui, an annual tribute student. His mother was née Wang. His parents and at least one grandparent were living. His younger brothers were Chongyu and Chongdun. He married a woman née Cao. He placed eighty-second in the Shuntian Prefecture Provincial Examination and two hundred seventy-eighth in the Metropolitan Examination.

translation_en: Jin Xuezeng was registered in the civilian household register of Jining Subprefecture, Yanzhou Prefecture, Shandong, and was an additional-quota student at the subprefectural school. He specialized in the Classic of Changes. His courtesy name was Zilu; he was second in birth order, aged twenty-nine, and born on the third day of the second lunar month. His great-grandfather was Li, his grandfather Tang, and his father Xian, a prestige official; his mother was née Tian. His parents and grandparents were living. His elder brother, Xueyan, was an Associate Prefect. He married a woman née Zhou and subsequently a woman née Meng. He placed fifty-first in the Shandong Provincial Examination and one hundred thirty-third in the Metropolitan Examination.

title: 嘉靖二十三年進士登科錄
text:
列聖相承懋修文德
海宇乂安國家無
事朕以支末上承
天命入纘
寶位兹越二旬載矣
===
夫何連歲以来北
虜寇疆入我中國
若蹈無人之境殘
我天民前所未有
本之以朕罔德基

… the successive sage emperors devoted themselves to cultivating civil virtue. All within the seas enjoyed peace and order, and the realm was free of troubles. I, from a collateral branch of the imperial family, received Heaven’s mandate and succeeded to the precious throne. Twenty years have now passed.

title: 嘉靖二十三年進士登科錄
text:
之立于中是以教
化莫克行于外者
也然朕又聞之曰
帝王之政守在四
夷今朕欲求長治
===
久安之術無出於
守之一端欲得其
守之之道當何施
用以盡其長且久
焉尔多士抱經世

punctuated: 之立于中，是以教化莫克行于外者也。然朕又聞之曰：「帝王之政，守在四夷。」今朕欲求長治久安之術，無出於守之一端。欲得其守之之道，當何施用，以盡其長且久焉？尔多士抱經世
translation_en: … established at the center [?], and thus moral instruction cannot be carried out beyond it. Yet I have also heard it said: “In the government of emperors and kings, defense lies among the barbarians of the four quarters.” Now I wish to seek the means of securing lasting order and enduring peace; nothing surpasses defense. To find the proper way to defend the realm, what measures should be employed to make that order and peace endure to the fullest? You assembled scholars harbor plans for ordering the world…

===
嘉靖二十三年三月十五日

之畧亦看日矣宜
各著于篇朕將采
而行之毋忌毋隱
===
嘉靖二十三年三月十五日
punctuated:
之畧亦有日矣。宜各著于篇，朕將采而行之，毋忌毋隱。

嘉靖二十三年三月十五日。
translation_en:
…have possessed plans for ordering the world for some time. Each of you should set them down in writing. I shall select from them and put them into practice. Have no misgivings and conceal nothing.

The fifteenth day of the third month of the twenty-third year of Jiajing (1544).

title: 嘉靖二十三年進士登科錄
text:
臣秦鳴雷
臣對臣聞帝王保大業於無疆者有經國之
規摸有植國之根本規摸之經也存乎法根
本之植也存乎仁是故崇文詰武經制豫定
使夫法之行於天下者整飭而不可紊夫是
之謂規摸脩德行仁膏澤下究使夫仁之洽
於人心者固結而不可解夫是之謂根本經
制定則國威立德澤究則國脉固由是萬姓
胥悅於域中聲教四訖於海外大業之保蓋
卓乎其不可拔矣自古帝王享國長久之道
===
何能外是二者苟法矣而未仁則品式雖周
而所以綱維之者無其本仁矣而無法則恩
意雖篤而所以經綸之者無其具是謂治之
偏而弗會其全始雖善而終流於弊將何以
保基圖之固而綿國祚之永也哉欽惟
皇帝陛下中和建極仁孝作孚
德化洽於民心而萬邦時憲
神武布於海宇而四夷来賓纘
列祖之鴻圖貽百世之燕翼太平有道之長端有

translation_en:
Your servant Qin Minglei.

Your servant replies: I have heard that emperors and kings who preserve their great enterprise without end have a framework for governing the state and a foundation upon which to establish it. Ordering that framework depends upon laws; planting that foundation depends upon benevolence. Thus, they exalt civil culture and put military affairs in order, establishing governing institutions beforehand, so that laws operate throughout the realm in an orderly fashion that cannot be disrupted. This is what is meant by the framework. They cultivate virtue and practice benevolence, extending their beneficence to those below, so that benevolence permeates the people's hearts and binds them inseparably together. This is what is meant by the foundation. When governing institutions are established, the state's authority stands firm; when virtuous beneficence reaches everywhere, the state's lifeblood is secure. Thus all the people rejoice within the realm, and its civilizing influence reaches in every direction beyond the seas. The preservation of the great enterprise is then assured, firmly beyond uprooting. Since ancient times, how could the way by which emperors and kings long maintain their states lie outside these two things?

If there are laws but no benevolence, then, although regulations and procedures are comprehensive, what holds them together lacks a foundation. If there is benevolence but no law, then, although kindly intentions are sincere, there are no instruments with which to order affairs. This is government that is one-sided and fails to embrace the whole. Though good at the outset, it ultimately degenerates into abuses. How, then, could it secure the foundations of imperial rule and perpetuate the dynasty's allotted span?

I reverently consider how Your Majesty the Emperor establishes the supreme standard through equilibrium and harmony, and inspires trust through benevolence and filial piety. Your transforming virtue permeates the people's hearts, and the myriad states take it as their model; your divine martial prowess extends throughout the realm, and the peoples of the four quarters come to pay homage. You carry forward the grand enterprise of your imperial ancestors and bequeath provision for peace to a hundred generations. title: 嘉靖二十三年進士登科錄
text:
今日矣乃尤不自滿假特進臣等于
廷策以禦夷之道且欲求夫長治久安之術是
豈徒以脩舉故事焉哉誠以草茅之下必有
明習文武大猷可以裨補治體者而臣非其
人也然臣即是有以仰窺
陛下望道未見求治若渴之盛心矣敢不粲之經
傳酌之時宜俛攄愚見以對揚
明詔於萬一乎臣嘗考之易曰鼓萬物而不與
聖人同憂天道也書曰天佑下民作之君作
之師惟其克相上帝寵綏四方則知天雖以
===
生物為心而理物之責不能不望于君君之
茂膺天眷也非徒肆於民上實以君師之道
存乎我而代之理也則凡斯民之安危利病
世道之否泰盛衰凡可以克盡其道而奠天
下於文熙武謐之域者自有不容於不講矣
今夫立天之道曰陰與陽立人之道曰仁與
義而帝王也者又所以法天而圖治者也是
故帝王以仁育天下非文無以昭休明之治
故凡崇獎儒彦懷保黔黎與夫體國經野明
物章軌以成經緯之德者皆文之屬也帝王

…the present day. Yet Your Majesty remains far from complacent: you have specially summoned us to court and examined us on the way to repel the foreign peoples, seeking also the means of lasting good government and enduring peace. Could this be merely a matter of observing established precedent? Surely it is because among those living in obscurity there must be men thoroughly versed in the great principles of civil and military governance who can contribute to the proper ordering of government. Your servant, however, is not such a man. Nevertheless, from this I can glimpse Your Majesty’s earnest resolve: you look toward the Way as though you had not yet seen it, and thirst for good government. How could I fail to elucidate these matters through the classics and their commentaries [?], weigh them against present circumstances, and humbly set forth my shallow views, so as to respond to even a tiny part of your enlightened edict? Your servant has examined this in the classics. The Book of Changes says: “To quicken the myriad things without sharing the sage’s cares is the Way of Heaven.” The Book of Documents says: “Heaven aids the people below, making rulers and teachers for them, that they may assist the Lord on High in cherishing and bringing peace to the four quarters.” Thus we know that although Heaven’s intention is to give life to all things, it must look to the ruler to take responsibility for ordering them. The ruler’s abundant receipt of Heaven’s favor is not merely a license to hold sway over the people. Rather, the duties of ruler and teacher rest in him, and he governs on Heaven’s behalf. Therefore, whatever concerns the people’s security or peril, benefit or suffering, and the world’s adversity or prosperity, flourishing or decline—every means of fully discharging those duties and settling the realm in civil prosperity and military tranquility—must necessarily be investigated.
Now, what establishes the Way of Heaven is called yin and yang; what establishes the Way of humanity is called benevolence and righteousness. Emperors and kings, moreover, take Heaven as their model in seeking good government. Thus, when emperors and kings nurture the realm through benevolence, only civil governance can manifest the excellence of enlightened rule. Accordingly, honoring and encouraging eminent Confucian scholars, cherishing and protecting the common people, organizing the capital and laying out the countryside, distinguishing things and making their proper regulations clear, thereby realizing the virtue that orders the whole—all these belong to civil governance. title: 嘉靖二十三年進士登科錄
text:
以義正天下非武無以示撻伐之威故凡選
擇将帥振勵卒徒與夫誅暴禁亂飭法嚴備
以成安定之功者皆武之屬也文以敷德則
海宇奠而内順治武以示威則疆圉靜而外
威嚴此誠有國家者不容以偏廢者也使有
武而無文以濟之則義勝而流於剛其何以
敦渾厚之治體有文而無武以濟之則仁勝
而流於懦又何以立精明之治功也哉乃若
召公之告康王曰張皇六師周公之告成王
曰其克詰爾戎兵此其爲言若有所偏者而
===
不知亂者保其治者也危者保其安者也是
揚武者乃所以覲文初非好於用兵也一或
講之無素備之弗豫則所以爲防者必疎而
其爲累也亦必不小是誠不容以或後者也
臣聞中國之有夷狄猶陽之有陰晝之有夜
君子之有小人不能以必去焉者也是故先
王建國列之侯封采服之外所以峻其防焉
號令不及其人正朔不加其國所以别其類
焉刑以懲叛禮以懷来所以服其心焉柰之
何狼子野心非我族類重以消長之勢無常

臣聞中國之有夷狄，猶陽之有陰、晝之有夜、君子之有小人，不能以必去焉者也。是故先王建國，列之侯封采服之外，所以峻其防焉；號令不及其人，正朔不加其國，所以别其類焉；刑以懲叛，禮以懷来，所以服其心焉。柰之何狼子野心，非我族類，重以消長之勢無常，
translation_en:
…rectify All under Heaven through righteousness, yet without military power they have no means of displaying the might of punitive expeditions. Thus selecting generals and commanders, encouraging the troops, punishing the violent and suppressing disorder, enforcing laws and maintaining strict defenses—all that accomplishes the work of securing peace—belong to the military sphere. When civil governance spreads virtue, the realm is settled and its interior obedient and well governed; when military power displays might, the frontiers are tranquil and authority abroad is imposing. These are truly things that those who possess a state cannot allow themselves to neglect on either side. If there were military power without civil governance to complement it, righteousness would predominate and lapse into harshness: how could this cultivate a generous and magnanimous form of government? If there were civil governance without military power to complement it, benevolence would predominate and lapse into weakness: how, then, could this establish the achievements of discerning and effective government?
As for the Duke of Shao telling King Kang, “Magnify the majesty of the Six Armies,” and the Duke of Zhou telling King Cheng, “Be sure to put your military forces in order,” these words might seem to favor one side. Yet such a reading fails to understand that disorder is what preserves order, and danger is what preserves security. Thus exalting military power serves to manifest civil virtue [?]; it is by no means a matter of delighting in warfare. Should military affairs not be studied routinely, and preparations not be made beforehand, defenses will inevitably be lax, and the harm they occasion will certainly be considerable. This is truly something that must never be put off.
Your servant has heard that the presence of the Yi and Di peoples alongside the Central States is like yin accompanying yang, night accompanying day, and petty men accompanying gentlemen: one cannot expect to eliminate them altogether. Therefore, when the former kings established their states, they placed these peoples beyond the domains of the regional lords and the territories of the granted estates, thereby making the barriers against them strict. Their commands did not extend to these peoples, nor was their calendar imposed upon their countries, thereby distinguishing their kind. Punishments chastised rebellion, while ritual courtesies welcomed those who came in submission, thereby winning over their hearts. Yet what can be done when they have the wild hearts of wolf cubs and are not of our kind, compounded by the inconstancy of the forces of decline and growth…

title: 嘉靖二十三年進士登科錄
text:
強弱之機莫測值其弱則稽顙而稱臣當其
強則犯順而干紀蓋自古則然矣故有化足
以成風動而不免於有苗之征德足以臻時
乂而不免於鬼方之伐治足以致中興而不
免於獫狁之孔熾是又奚足爲盛世之累哉
故曰帝王不患有夷狄之強而患吾無禦之
之具不貴有禦夷之具而貴吾無以致夷之
窺而已矣強本以治內嚴兵以固圉来則必
治去則不追務使各安其所而不敢干吾治
者茲非計之良乎三代以降此道則寢微矣
===
嬴秦命将出師築塞以禦強胡糜費巨萬夷
患未袪而國釁已不可救矣是謂虛內以事
外漢武以雄才大略之資爲窮追遠討之舉
登南臺於塞北絕王庭於幕南夷氛雖息而
民生已不勝困矣是謂計末而忘本斯皆策
之最下者也他如唐稱臣於突厥既病貽謀
之不臧宋迫辱於遼金復患脩攘之坐失是
又幾於無策矣安得而不淪胥以致茲極乎
幸而
天啓

強弱之機莫測。值其弱，則稽顙而稱臣；當其強，則犯順而干紀。蓋自古則然矣。故有化足以成風動，而不免於有苗之征；德足以臻時乂，而不免於鬼方之伐；治足以致中興，而不免於獫狁之孔熾。是又奚足爲盛世之累哉？故曰：帝王不患有夷狄之強，而患吾無禦之之具；不貴有禦夷之具，而貴吾無以致夷之窺而已矣。強本以治內，嚴兵以固圉，来則必治，去則不追，務使各安其所而不敢干吾治者，茲非計之良乎？三代以降，此道則寢微矣。

…and the turns of strength and weakness are impossible to predict. When weak, they bow their foreheads to the ground and acknowledge themselves as subjects; when strong, they defy legitimate authority and violate the established order. This has been so since antiquity. Thus, even a transforming influence sufficient to move the people as the wind moves grass did not obviate the campaign against the Youmiao; virtue sufficient to bring about good order did not obviate the expedition against the Guifang; and government sufficient to achieve a dynastic restoration did not prevent the Xianyun from becoming exceedingly formidable. How, then, could this alone count as a blemish upon a flourishing age? Hence the saying: emperors and kings do not worry that the foreign peoples are strong, but that we lack the means to resist them. Nor do they prize merely possessing the means to resist them; rather, they prize giving them no occasion to covet our territory. Strengthen the foundations to maintain order within; keep the troops disciplined to secure the frontiers. When invaders come, punish them without fail; when they withdraw, do not pursue them. Strive to ensure that each remains content in its own territory and dares not disrupt our order. Is this not a sound policy? Since the Three Dynasties, this way has gradually declined.
The Qin rulers of the Ying house ordered generals to lead armies forth and built frontier fortifications to resist the powerful Hu, squandering enormous sums. Before the foreign threat had been removed, the troubles within their own state had already become irreparable. This is called draining the interior to attend to external affairs. Emperor Wu of Han, endowed with heroic talent and grand strategic vision, undertook relentless pursuits and distant expeditions. He ascended the Southern Terrace north of the frontier [?] and eliminated the royal court south of the desert. Although the foreign menace subsided, the people's livelihood had already been subjected to unbearable hardship. This is called attending to the branches while forgetting the root. These were all policies of the lowest order. title: 嘉靖二十三年進士登科錄
text:
皇明我
聖祖高皇帝以天縱之聖奮起淮甸迅掃腥羶驅
之北歸絕其南冦建自古所未有之事功復
帝王所自立之中國
神謨勇略固嘗以武功定天下矣至于
即位之始干戈甫息乃欲偃武脩文以德化天

…the august Ming. Our sagely progenitor, Emperor Gao, endowed by Heaven with sagehood, rose in the Huai region, swiftly swept away the rank and foul-smelling enemy, drove them back north, and ended their incursions into the south. He accomplished feats without precedent since antiquity and restored the Central Realm in which emperors and kings had established their rule. Through divine counsels and courageous strategy, he had indeed pacified All under Heaven by military achievement. Yet at the beginning of his reign, when warfare had only just ceased, he wished to lay down arms, cultivate civil governance, and transform All under Heaven through virtue. Why was this? Because the realm had only recently been pacified: to support the wounded, sustain those in peril, and allow All under Heaven to rest and recover, surely no course took precedence over this. It was certainly not that he had resolved to forget warfare. Consider how he anticipated dangers and guarded against them, leaving earnest and emphatic instructions: how profound and far-reaching were his measures to establish an unshakable foundation and bequeath guiding principles to his descendants!
Thereupon our Chengzu three times set forth in his imperial carriage drawn by six steeds, again displaying the might of punitive campaigns. Down to the successive sage emperors, they nurtured their military prestige, strengthened defenses, and never forgot strategies for keeping the enemy under control. How enlightened and comprehensive, too, were their measures to perpetuate the dynasty’s enduring fortune while scrupulously observing established precedents!
Reverently considering Your Majesty, you possess divinely enlightened virtue and have come at a time of dynastic resurgence. title: 嘉靖二十三年進士登科錄
text:
神孫後先相望
盛德大業篤祜無疆
國家長治久安之術尚何以他求為哉雖然帝
王望治之心無窮人臣愛君之心無已故古
稱大舜之知必曰好問好察彼賈誼當文帝
之世猶有取於厝火積薪之喻焉則臣雖至
愚所以仰稱
德意而自靖厥忠者可終默焉而已乎臣請得
而籌之夫王者以京師為室以諸夏為庭户
以四夷為藩籬其內外遠近之分先後緩急
===
之序盖不待較而知也粤自先王寓兵於農
之意既壞而後世制馭之道不容不分要之
厚民所以足兵恤兵所以衛民實相資而非
相病也然則端本自治之道夫亦於二者而
加之意乎以今日之民言之安其田里施之
教化殿最書于臺臣而守牧有考利病關於
藩臬而興革以時以至水旱凶災之必聞賑
貸蠲免之屢下是
陛下所以厚民者無不盡也以今日之兵言之歲
給之衣月給之糧額籍總於司馬而逃亡可

神孫，後先相望，盛德大業，篤祜無疆。國家長治久安之術，尚何以他求為哉？雖然，帝王望治之心無窮，人臣愛君之心無已。故古稱大舜之知，必曰好問好察。彼賈誼當文帝之世，猶有取於厝火積薪之喻焉。則臣雖至愚，所以仰稱德意而自靖厥忠者，可終默焉而已乎？臣請得而籌之。
夫王者以京師為室，以諸夏為庭户，以四夷為藩籬，其內外遠近之分、先後緩急之序，盖不待較而知也。粤自先王寓兵於農之意既壞，而後世制馭之道不容不分。要之，厚民所以足兵，恤兵所以衛民，實相資而非相病也。然則端本自治之道，夫亦於二者而加之意乎？
以今日之民言之，安其田里，施之教化，殿最書于臺臣而守牧有考，利病關於藩臬而興革以時，以至水旱凶災之必聞、賑貸蠲免之屢下，是陛下所以厚民者無不盡也。以今日之兵言之，歲給之衣，月給之糧，額籍總於司馬而逃亡可
translation_en:
…and the divine descendant, answering one another across the generations: their splendid virtue and great achievements bring abundant blessings without end. What further need is there to seek elsewhere the means of securing lasting order and enduring peace for the realm? Nevertheless, an emperor’s desire for good government knows no bounds, and a minister’s devotion to his sovereign never ceases. Thus, when the ancients praised the wisdom of the great Shun, they invariably spoke of his fondness for questioning and examining closely. Even Jia Yi, living under Emperor Wen, found occasion to use the analogy of placing fire beneath a pile of firewood. Though your servant is utterly foolish, can I simply remain silent forever, if I am to answer Your Majesty’s virtuous intentions and fulfill my loyalty with a clear conscience? Allow your servant to consider the matter.
A true king takes the capital as his chamber, the Chinese domains as his courtyard and doorway, and the peoples of the four quarters as his enclosing fence. The distinctions between inner and outer, near and far, and the order of precedence and urgency are surely evident without comparison. Once the former kings’ principle of embedding the soldiery among the farmers had broken down, later generations necessarily had to distinguish their methods of governing the people and controlling the troops. In essence, providing generously for the people makes adequate provision for the army possible; caring for the troops serves to protect the people. The two support, rather than impair, one another. Should not the way of setting the foundations right and putting our own affairs in order therefore consist in giving attention to both?
As for the people today, they are settled securely in their fields and villages and receive moral instruction. Censorial officials record the lowest and highest assessments, so that prefects and other local administrators are evaluated; matters of benefit and harm are reported to the provincial administration and surveillance commissions, so that measures are introduced or abolished at the appropriate time. Even floods, droughts, and other calamities must be reported, while orders for relief, loans, and tax remissions are repeatedly issued. Thus Your Majesty has left nothing undone in providing generously for the people. As for the troops today, they receive clothing annually and grain monthly. Registers of authorized troop strengths are consolidated under the Minister of War, so that deserters can be…

習之有方賞罰鼓舞之無倦是
陛下所以恤兵者無遺策也夫民安而本益以固
兵精而氣益以振是宜勢益以昌威益以遠
文熈而武益以謐也然而北虜之窺伺猶昨
邊境之烽火繹聞頃者入我中國若蹈無人
之境誠有如
聖諭所及者此其故何也臣愚以為
聖心之憂民至矣而所以宣力於下者或非其良
聖政之養兵善矣而所以分閫於外者或非其寄

Even the organization and training of troops follow proper methods, while rewards and punishments are tirelessly used to spur them on. Thus Your Majesty has left no measure untried in caring for the troops. When the people are at peace, the foundations become ever firmer; when the troops are well trained, their spirit rises ever higher. Accordingly, the strength of the realm should flourish increasingly, its awe-inspiring power extend ever farther, civil affairs prosper, and military affairs become ever more tranquil. title: 嘉靖二十三年進士登科錄
text:
守是投之以可乘之隙守之未見其固也士
氣未張而應敵以戰是先之以可敗之道戰
之未見其利也然則長治久安之術抑何以
他求焉哉亦惟重守令之任而選之也必精
使郡縣之布列皆龔黃卓魯其人焉于是嚴
黜陟之典申久任之規勞心撫字必增秩以
示榮奉職無聞必奪爵以示辱塞奔競僥倖
之門斥闒茸貪墨之吏如是則民安而無復
失所之歎矣重將帥之任而簡之也必慎使
閫外之分據皆頗牧韓范其人焉于是專委
===
任之託昭勸懲之典有功必賞寬之以歲月
之餘有罪必誅略之以文法之細無以一人
之譽而尚其賢無以盈篋之謗而撓其志如
是則兵精而咸起報効之思矣由是而昭武
勇以示威脩戰備以利用謹關隘以辯姦遠
間諜以防詐嚴吾之守以俟敵之戰將見投
之無釁覘之無隙虜知吾之有守矣以靜制
動以逸待勞虜屈吾之不戰矣茲固帝王萬
全之策古今不易之道也尚何夷患之足憂
耶否則翫寇輕敵其禍大邀功生事其計危

punctuated: 守，是投之以可乘之隙，守之未見其固也。士氣未張而應敵以戰，是先之以可敗之道，戰之未見其利也。然則長治久安之術，抑何以他求焉哉？亦惟重守令之任，而選之也必精，使郡縣之布列皆龔黃卓魯其人焉。于是嚴黜陟之典，申久任之規，勞心撫字，必增秩以示榮；奉職無聞，必奪爵以示辱。塞奔競僥倖之門，斥闒茸貪墨之吏，如是則民安而無復失所之歎矣。重將帥之任，而簡之也必慎，使閫外之分據皆頗牧韓范其人焉。于是專委任之託，昭勸懲之典，有功必賞，寬之以歲月之餘；有罪必誅，略之以文法之細。無以一人之譽而尚其賢，無以盈篋之謗而撓其志。如是則兵精而咸起報効之思矣。由是而昭武勇以示威，脩戰備以利用，謹關隘以辯姦，遠間諜以防詐，嚴吾之守以俟敵之戰，將見投之無釁，覘之無隙，虜知吾之有守矣。以靜制動，以逸待勞，虜屈吾之不戰矣。茲固帝王萬全之策，古今不易之道也，尚何夷患之足憂耶？否則翫寇輕敵，其禍大；邀功生事，其計危。
translation_en:
…defense: this gives the enemy an opening to exploit; I cannot see how such defense can be secure. To engage the enemy in battle before the soldiers’ morale has been roused is to set out upon a path to defeat; I cannot see how such fighting can be advantageous. Where else, then, should one seek the means of lasting good government and enduring peace? One need only attach due importance to the responsibilities of prefects and county magistrates and select them with utmost care, so that those stationed throughout the prefectures and counties are all men like Gong Sui, Huang Ba, Zhuo Mao, and Lu Gong. Then rigorously enforce the rules for dismissal and promotion, and reaffirm the provisions for long tenure. Those who devote themselves to nurturing the people must receive higher rank as a mark of honor; those whose service brings no noteworthy achievement must be stripped of their rank as a mark of disgrace. Close the avenues to competitive self-advancement and undeserved preferment, and dismiss base, incompetent, and corrupt officials. In this way the people will be secure, and no longer lament that they have lost their proper place.

Attach due importance to the responsibilities of military commanders and choose them with utmost caution, so that those holding commands in the field are all men like Lian Po, Li Mu, Han Qi, and Fan Zhongyan. Then entrust them fully with their commands and make clear the rules for encouragement and punishment. Merit must be rewarded, and they must be allowed ample time; guilt must be punished, while petty technicalities of legal procedure should be overlooked. Do not exalt a man’s worth on the strength of one person’s praise, or undermine his resolve because of a chestful of slanders. In this way the troops will become proficient, and all will be moved to repay the sovereign through service.

Proceed, therefore, to display martial courage to manifest your might, put military preparations in order to ensure effective action, guard the passes carefully to distinguish malefactors, and keep spies at a distance to prevent deception. Make our defenses rigorous and await the enemy’s attack. Then the enemy will find no breach to strike at and no opening to discover by reconnaissance, and will know that we are well defended. By controlling movement through stillness and awaiting the weary while ourselves at ease, we shall subdue the enemy without fighting. This is indeed the sovereign’s policy of complete security, the way that has remained unchanged from antiquity to the present. What cause, then, is there to fear troubles from foreign peoples? Otherwise, to treat raiders carelessly and underestimate the enemy brings great calamity; to provoke incidents in pursuit of merit is a perilous plan…

皆非臣之所敢知也雖然禦夷之道固在於
治內而治內之要莫切於治心故心存於正
則事無不正而天下蒙其福心蔽於邪則事
無不邪而天下與其憂
陛下紹心學之傳發道統之秘
敬一有箴四箴有註所以預養此心者固已能
自得師矣臣恒慮操持之甚難察識之不易
耳夫人主深居九重攻之者衆倘於防微杜
漸之戒省察克治之功一未至焉臣恐虛明
湛一之體有不能復如其初矣臣願
===
陛下戒之慎之明通公溥以植其本靜虛動直以
培其基戒謹於不睹不聞之時察識於內外
賓主之辨親賢遠佞俾一暴弗替於十寒慎
終如始使九仞罔虧於一簣淫哇之聲奇巧
之色則曰吾心之賊也便嬖之言側媚之態
則曰吾心之蠹也土木遊田之娛宮室侈靡
之奉則曰吾心之所以喪失而不自覺者也
兢兢如堯業業如舜孜孜如禹慄慄如湯亦
保亦臨如文不泄不忘如武則心存而德可
脩德脩而道可立道立而政可舉由是顯設

punctuated:
皆非臣之所敢知也。雖然，禦夷之道固在於治內，而治內之要莫切於治心。故心存於正，則事無不正，而天下蒙其福；心蔽於邪，則事無不邪，而天下與其憂。
陛下紹心學之傳，發道統之秘，《敬一》有箴，《四箴》有註，所以預養此心者，固已能自得師矣。臣恒慮操持之甚難，察識之不易耳。夫人主深居九重，攻之者衆。倘於防微杜漸之戒、省察克治之功，一未至焉，臣恐虛明湛一之體，有不能復如其初矣。
臣願陛下戒之慎之，明通公溥以植其本，靜虛動直以培其基。戒謹於不睹不聞之時，察識於內外賓主之辨。親賢遠佞，俾一暴弗替於十寒；慎終如始，使九仞罔虧於一簣。淫哇之聲、奇巧之色，則曰：「吾心之賊也。」便嬖之言、側媚之態，則曰：「吾心之蠹也。」土木遊田之娛、宮室侈靡之奉，則曰：「吾心之所以喪失而不自覺者也。」兢兢如堯，業業如舜，孜孜如禹，慄慄如湯，亦保亦臨如文，不泄不忘如武，則心存而德可脩，德脩而道可立，道立而政可舉。由是顯設…
translation_en:
…none of these are courses your servant would dare countenance. Nevertheless, the way to repel the barbarians certainly lies in putting affairs at home in order, and nothing is more essential to this than governing the mind. Thus, when the mind abides in rectitude, every undertaking is upright, and all under Heaven receive its blessings; when the mind is obscured by perversity, every undertaking is perverse, and all under Heaven share its troubles.
Your Majesty has continued the transmission of the learning of the mind and revealed the mysteries of the succession of the Way. You have composed an Admonition on Reverent Oneness and a commentary on the Four Admonitions. In thus nurturing the mind beforehand, you have indeed already found a teacher within yourself. Your servant is constantly concerned only that maintaining one's hold upon it is exceedingly difficult, and discerning its workings is not easy. The ruler dwells deep within the ninefold palace gates, yet those who assail his mind are many. If there is even one shortcoming in vigilance against the slightest beginnings of evil, or in the work of introspection and self-mastery, your servant fears that the mind's essential emptiness, luminosity, clarity, and unity may no longer be restored to their original condition.
Your servant wishes Your Majesty to be watchful and cautious in this: establish the roots through clear understanding and all-embracing impartiality; strengthen the foundation by remaining empty in stillness and upright in action. Be vigilant and cautious even when nothing is seen or heard, and discern the distinction between inner and outer, guest and host. Draw close to the worthy and keep flatterers at a distance, so that one day's exposure to warmth is not undone by ten days of cold. Be as careful at the end as at the beginning, so that a mound nine ren high is not left unfinished for want of a single basket of earth. Of licentious, debased music and sights of ingenious artifice, say: “These are robbers of my mind.” Of the words of intimate favorites and the bearing of obsequious flatterers, say: “These are worms that eat away at my mind.” Of the pleasures of building, excursions, and hunting, and the provision of extravagant palaces, say: “These are what cause me to lose my mind's integrity without realizing it.” Be vigilant like Yao, circumspect like Shun, diligent like Yu, and fearful like Tang; preserve and watch over the realm like King Wen, and be neither remiss nor forgetful like King Wu. Then, with the mind preserved, virtue can be cultivated; with virtue cultivated, the Way can be established; with the Way established, government can be carried out. From this, it will be manifestly displayed…

title: 嘉靖二十三年進士登科錄
text:
於
朝廷而庶事康矣
頒布於四海而萬民樂矣洋溢於蠻陌而四夷
慕矣天地位萬物育諸福之物可致之祥莫
不畢至而王道終矣此非臣之臆說也伯益
之戒舜曰無怠無荒四夷來王漢儒董仲舒
曰正心以正朝廷正朝廷以正百官而宋儒
朱熹亦謂其本不在威強而在德業其任不
在邊境而在朝廷其具不在兵食而在紀綱
此端本之道古今一致而實臣愚之所惓望
===
於
今日者也惟
陛下不棄芻蕘
留神省覽見之施行則
宗社幸甚天下幸甚臣干冒
天威戰慄無地不勝惓惓仰望之至臣謹對

天威戰慄無地不勝惓惓仰望之至臣謹對
punctuated:
於朝廷，而庶事康矣；頒布於四海，而萬民樂矣；洋溢於蠻陌，而四夷慕矣。天地位，萬物育，諸福之物、可致之祥，莫不畢至，而王道終矣。此非臣之臆說也。伯益之戒舜曰：「無怠無荒，四夷來王。」漢儒董仲舒曰：「正心以正朝廷，正朝廷以正百官。」而宋儒朱熹亦謂：「其本不在威強而在德業，其任不在邊境而在朝廷，其具不在兵食而在紀綱。」此端本之道，古今一致，而實臣愚之所惓望於今日者也。
惟陛下不棄芻蕘，留神省覽，見之施行，則宗社幸甚，天下幸甚！臣干冒天威，戰慄無地，不勝惓惓仰望之至。臣謹對。
translation_en:
…at court, and all affairs will prosper; promulgated throughout the realm, it will bring joy to all the people; spreading abundantly among the distant peoples [?], it will win the admiration of the peoples of the four quarters. Heaven and earth will take their proper places, and the myriad things will flourish. All things that bring blessings and all auspicious signs that may be elicited will arrive together, and the Kingly Way will attain its fulfillment. These are not your servant’s conjectures. Bo Yi admonished Shun: “Be neither idle nor neglectful, and the peoples of the four quarters will come to acknowledge you as king.” The Han scholar Dong Zhongshu said: “Rectify your heart to rectify the court; rectify the court to rectify the hundred officials.” The Song scholar Zhu Xi likewise stated: “Its foundation lies in virtuous achievement, not coercive might; responsibility for it lies at court, not on the frontiers; its means lie in governing principles and discipline, not troops and provisions.” This way of rectifying the foundation has been consistent from antiquity to the present, and it is truly what your foolish servant earnestly hopes for today.
If only Your Majesty will not reject these humble words of a grass cutter and wood gatherer, but attend to and examine them, and put them into practice, the dynastic ancestral temples and altars of soil and grain will be most fortunate, and all under Heaven most fortunate! Your servant has presumptuously offended Your heavenly majesty; trembling with fear and finding no place to stand, I cannot contain my utmost earnest hope as I look up to You. Your servant respectfully submits this reply.

title: 嘉靖二十三年進士登科錄
text:
臣瞿景淳
臣對臣聞帝王之御天下也有致治之大法
有善治之大幾文武者致治之大法也文武
之用各惟其時者善治之大幾也帝王之受
命于天而統理華夷也觀天之有陽而文教
興焉是文也者所以象天之生育也觀天之
有陰而武備脩焉是武也者所以象天之震
曜也然創業之初不患無武而患文教之或
微守成之日不患無文而患武功之弗競所
貴乎善治者亦隨時張弛使適于治而已矣
===
是故知大法則天下之治並行而不悖知大
幾則天下之治善救而不窮古之帝王所以
不動聲色而奠宗社于泰山之安者由此其
選也恭惟
皇帝陛下躬神聖之資撫盈成之運秉
離照以宣文則有以成
文明之治奮
乾剛而用武則有以張
震疊之威如臣者蓋亦沐浴膏澤歌咏太平而蕩
蕩其難名矣廼于

translation_en:
Your servant Qu Jingchun.
Your servant replies: I have heard that when emperors and kings govern the realm, there are great principles for bringing about order and crucial judgments on which good government turns. Civil and military measures are the great principles for bringing about order; employing each at its proper time is the crucial judgment on which good government turns. When emperors and kings receive Heaven’s mandate and govern the Chinese and the peoples beyond, they observe Heaven’s yang and promote civil instruction: civil measures thus emulate Heaven’s generation and nurturing of life. They observe Heaven’s yin and put military preparations in order: military measures thus emulate Heaven’s thunderous, dazzling might. Yet at the founding of a dynasty, the concern is not a lack of military strength but the possible weakness of civil instruction; when preserving an established dynasty, the concern is not a lack of civil cultivation but inadequate military achievement. What is valued in good government is simply tightening or relaxing measures as the times require, making them conducive to order. Thus, understanding the great principles allows the means of governing the realm to operate together without conflict; understanding the crucial judgments allows government to remedy deficiencies effectively without exhausting its resources. That the emperors and kings of antiquity could, without raising their voices or changing their expressions, establish the ancestral temples and the altars of soil and grain as securely as Mount Tai was due to their choice of this course [?].
I reverently reflect that Your Majesty the Emperor possesses divine and sagely endowments and presides over an age of full achievement. Wielding the illumination of Li to spread civil culture, you have the means to achieve enlightened government; rousing the firmness of Qian to employ military force, you have the means to display awe-inspiring might. title: 嘉靖二十三年進士登科錄
text:
萬幾之暇特進臣等于
廷俯
賜清問上嘉
祖宗致治之盛下求
今日保治之方且
諭臣等以守之之道詳著于篇臣雖愚陋有以仰
窺
聖心之純有不以
今日治安爲已足直欲建萬世之長策保
大業于無疆矣夫堯舜之聖尚有蠻夷猾夏之憂
===
則今兹北虜亦何足以累
聖治乎然臣聞之四郊多壘卿大夫之辱也執干
戈以衛社稷者亦士之任也則今邊鄙多聳
穡人無功凡吾臣子皆與有責矣臣敢不罄
一得之愚以答千載之遇乎夫帝王之御天
下以成久安長治之術者無他惟文武二途
而已矣顧其爲道也不可易而其爲用也不
可齊文教之綏所以求内之順治也一于文
而不知有武則禍亂無所于定而或以廢天
下之功武衛之奮所以求外之威嚴也一于

…amid the respite from Your Majesty’s myriad affairs of state, you specially summoned us, your servants, to court and graciously bestowed your august questions upon us. You praised the flourishing government achieved by your imperial ancestors and sought the means of preserving good government today. You also instructed us in the way to maintain it, setting this out fully in your text. Though ignorant and unrefined, I can thereby glimpse the purity of your sagely heart: you do not regard today’s good government and peace as sufficient, but wish to establish a lasting plan for ten thousand generations and preserve the great imperial enterprise forever. Even the sages Yao and Shun worried about the Man and Yi disturbing the central lands. How, then, could the northern barbarians of today detract from your sagely government? Yet I have heard it said: “When fortifications abound in the four outskirts, it is a disgrace to the ministers and grandees.” To take up shield and spear in defense of the altars of soil and grain is also the responsibility of a scholar. Now that the borderlands suffer frequent alarms and the farmers’ labors bear no fruit, all of us who serve as your subjects share responsibility. Dare I fail to exhaust my meager understanding in response to this opportunity granted once in a thousand years?

text:
武而不知有文則化理無所于飭而或以啓
天下之釁臣故曰道之不可易者此也然天
下之勢有強弱而文武之用有緩急開國之
初國勢爲強乘強之勢者利用文繼體之日
國勢爲弱乘弱之勢者利用武有武以濟文
之所不及則惠覃而不之玩有文以濟武之

…if one relies exclusively on military force and knows nothing of civil governance, moral transformation and good order have no means of being put into effect, and this may open the way to troubles throughout the realm. Thus your servant says: this is why their underlying principles cannot be altered. Yet the realm’s circumstances vary in strength and weakness, and the employment of civil and military means varies in urgency. At the founding of a dynasty, the state is strong; those acting from a position of strength benefit from employing civil means. Under succeeding rulers, the state is weak; those acting from a position of weakness benefit from employing military means. When military force supplements what civil governance cannot accomplish, beneficence spreads widely without being treated lightly. When civil governance supplements what military force cannot accomplish, authority inspires awe without crushing the people. Thus your servant says: this is why their employment cannot be uniform. Yet emperors and kings take the whole realm as their measure. In selecting generals, training troops, and employing military force when occasion requires, they do not seek victory over foreign peoples. We merely govern our own Central Realm and ensure that they do not disturb it. Civil governance is the state’s constant principle, the means by which it is maintained; military force is the state’s support, the means by which that maintenance is secured. Though their functions differ, they are one in tending toward good order. Thus your servant says: emperors and kings govern the realm through these two ways alone, the civil and the military.
I have reverently read the imperial decree, which states: “I consider that the civil and military ways must be employed together: neither may be omitted, nor may either be favored exclusively. The transmitted text says, ‘Make a mighty display of the Six Armies.’ It also says, ‘Be capable of putting your weapons and troops in order.’ Does this not indicate a fondness for employing troops?” How great are these imperial words! They surely reveal insight into the circumstances of the realm and mastery of the discretion required to tighten or relax measures. title: 嘉靖二十三年進士登科錄
text:
謨謀帷幄則爲敬義一德之訓有事而出總
戎行則爲升陔鷹揚之師是相亦將也以言
乎兵農無事而耕則爲比閭族黨之民有事
而戰則爲伍兩軍師之制是兵亦農也文武
之在昔未始分也自管敬仲以國中之民爲
兵以四郊之民爲農兵農始分而不可合矣
自宋人以樞密主兵中書主民將相始分而
不相統矣然兵以衛民民以養兵相主運籌
將主決戰體統相維中外相應後之帝王亦
未始獨任而成功者文武之在後世用之亦
===
未始偏也夫惟未始分也是故有渾融完固
之勢夫惟用之未始偏也是故有迭運不窮
之神譬之天道之陰陽雖慘舒各一其氣其
成歲功則一而已矣顧帝王所以制治于未
亂保邦于未危使天下之勢不至于極重而
難反者則有幾焉昔周公之輔成王也禮樂
之化致夫重譯蓋以文治爲先矣而克詰戎
兵之訓首迪于訪落之始召公之輔康王也
保釐之治洽于東郊蓋亦以文治爲先矣而
張皇六師之訓首陳于踐阼之初成康之爲

謨謀帷幄，則爲敬義一德之訓；有事而出總戎行，則爲升陔鷹揚之師，是相亦將也。以言乎兵農，無事而耕，則爲比閭族黨之民；有事而戰，則爲伍兩軍師之制，是兵亦農也。文武之在昔未始分也。自管敬仲以國中之民爲兵，以四郊之民爲農，兵農始分而不可合矣。自宋人以樞密主兵，中書主民，將相始分而不相統矣。然兵以衛民，民以養兵，相主運籌，將主決戰，體統相維，中外相應，後之帝王亦未始獨任而成功者。文武之在後世，用之亦未始偏也。
夫惟未始分也，是故有渾融完固之勢；夫惟用之未始偏也，是故有迭運不窮之神。譬之天道之陰陽，雖慘舒各一其氣，其成歲功則一而已矣。顧帝王所以制治于未亂，保邦于未危，使天下之勢不至于極重而難反者，則有幾焉。
昔周公之輔成王也，禮樂之化致夫重譯，蓋以文治爲先矣，而克詰戎兵之訓，首迪于訪落之始。召公之輔康王也，保釐之治洽于東郊，蓋亦以文治爲先矣，而張皇六師之訓，首陳于踐阼之初。成康之爲

…when devising plans within the command tent, they offered counsels of reverence, righteousness, and undivided virtue; when affairs arose and they went forth to command the ranks, theirs were armies that ascended Gai [?] and soared like hawks. Thus ministers were also generals. As for soldiers and farmers, when there was no conflict and they tilled the fields, they were the people organized into neighborhood units of bi, lü, zu, and dang; when conflict arose and they fought, they were organized into military units of wu, liang, jun, and shi. Thus soldiers were also farmers. In antiquity, the civil and military spheres were never separate. Once Guan Jingzhong made the inhabitants of the capital soldiers and those of the four outlying districts farmers, soldiers and farmers became separate and could no longer be united. Once the men of the Song dynasty put the Bureau of Military Affairs in charge of soldiers and the Secretariat in charge of the people, generals and ministers became separate and no longer exercised authority over one another. Yet soldiers protected the people, and the people supported the soldiers; ministers directed strategic planning, and generals directed decisive battles. Their institutions sustained one another, and the central and regional authorities responded to one another. Later emperors and kings likewise never achieved success by relying exclusively on either sphere. Thus, even in later ages, the employment of civil and military means was never one-sided.
Precisely because they were never separate, they possessed an integrated, complete, and secure configuration of power; precisely because their employment was never one-sided, they possessed the marvelous capacity to operate alternately without exhaustion. They may be compared to yin and yang in the Way of Heaven: although contraction and expansion each have their distinctive vital force, they are one in bringing the work of the year to completion. Yet there are incipient tendencies that emperors and kings must discern if they are to establish order before disorder arises, preserve the state before danger appears, and prevent the configuration of power in the realm from becoming so heavily weighted that it is difficult to reverse.
Formerly, when the Duke of Zhou assisted King Cheng, the transforming influence of rites and music brought people from afar who required successive interpreters. Clearly, civil government came first. Yet the admonition to put weapons and troops in good order was among his first instructions when the king began seeking counsel. When the Duke of Shao assisted King Kang, his administration for preserving order extended throughout the eastern outskirts. Here too, civil government clearly came first. 武功適其君者周治尚文其勢已弱而又當
豐亨豫大之時使不從武備之易隳者而振
勵之則以弱政濟弱勢四夷之交侵諸侯之
負固當不俟夫昭王之後而後見此臣所以
妄論天下之勢必識其幾而後可以善其治
于不窮也臣請以

列聖之所以紹休
今日之所以守天下者次第陳之可乎我
===
===

武功之盛蓋已震乎殊方矣而
登極之日首崇學校其治若先乎文我
成祖之繼天立極也親禮儒臣表章性理
文德之盛蓋已光于海隅矣而靖難之後三犁虜

武烈之所被者寔開其先矣今我

我皇祖之開天撫運也，驅策英豪，迅掃胡虜，武功之盛，蓋已震乎殊方矣。而登極之日，首崇學校，其治若先乎文。我成祖之繼天立極也，親禮儒臣，表章性理，文德之盛，蓋已光于海隅矣。而靖難之後，三犁虜庭，其治若先乎武。此固帝王補偏救弊之大權，未易以常情測者也。自是以來，列聖相承，大業益固。蓋雖文治之精華，而武烈之所被者寔開其先矣。今我
translation_en:
…as rulers, could they possibly have used military achievements to afflict their people? As ministers, could the Duke of Zhou and the Duke of Shao possibly have used military achievements to indulge their rulers? Zhou government esteemed civil culture, and its position had already weakened; moreover, this was a time of abundant prosperity and expansive ease. Had they failed to reinvigorate military preparations, which were easily allowed to deteriorate, weak government would have compounded a weak position. Invasions from all sides by the peoples beyond the realm and defiance by regional lords relying on their strongholds would have appeared without waiting until after King Zhao’s reign. This is why your servant ventures to argue that, in assessing the circumstances of the realm, one must discern the first intimations of change before one can govern it well without end. May your servant set forth in sequence how the Imperial Ancestor laid down the dynastic succession, how the successive sage emperors continued his glorious work, and how the realm is preserved today?
When our Imperial Ancestor inaugurated the dynasty and took charge of its appointed destiny, he directed heroes and swiftly swept away the northern foes. The grandeur of his military achievements had already awed distant lands. Yet upon ascending the throne, he gave foremost honor to schools: his government seemed to put civil culture first. When our Chengzu succeeded to Heaven’s mandate and established the supreme standard of rule, he personally honored Confucian ministers and promoted the learning of human nature and principle. The grandeur of his civil virtue had already shone to the farthest shores. Yet after the campaign to quell disorder, he three times plowed through the enemy’s court: his government seemed to put military affairs first. This was indeed the great discretionary power by which emperors correct imbalances and remedy abuses, something not readily fathomed by ordinary judgment. From that time onward, the successive sage emperors inherited the throne, and the great dynastic enterprise became ever more secure. 皇上以聖神文武之資致雍熈悠久之治盖二十
有三年于兹是故德之所及涵濡如雨露威
之所及震動如雷霆治之所及容保如天地
盖不止于西旅之貢獒越裳之獻雉也邇者
北虜遺孽乃忘我
天覆之仁哨聚入寇殘我天民有如
聖制所云者此固文武臣工奉行未至者之罪也
使文武臣工各供其職各效其能則干羽之
化既足以懷其携貳之心
廟算之勝又有以折其驕悍之氣撫之而易從征
===
之而易服矣今
陛下乃曰朕罔德基之立于中是以教化莫克行
于外此誠禹湯罪己之盛心也凡我臣工又
孰敢不祗承
德意而修其職分之所未盡者乎臣固知北虜
之不足平也伏讀

之之道當何施用以盡其長且久焉且

于外此誠禹湯罪己之盛心也凡我臣工又
之而易服矣今

之不足平也伏讀

之之道當何施用以盡其長且久焉且
誠臣等毋忌毋隱各著于篇臣雖不肖亦不敢上
punctuated:
皇上以聖神文武之資，致雍熈悠久之治，盖二十有三年于兹。是故德之所及，涵濡如雨露；威之所及，震動如雷霆；治之所及，容保如天地。盖不止于西旅之貢獒、越裳之獻雉也。邇者，北虜遺孽乃忘我天覆之仁，哨聚入寇，殘我天民，有如聖制所云者。此固文武臣工奉行未至者之罪也。使文武臣工各供其職，各效其能，則干羽之化既足以懷其携貳之心，廟算之勝又有以折其驕悍之氣，撫之而易從，征之而易服矣。今陛下乃曰：「朕罔德基之立于中，是以教化莫克行于外。」此誠禹湯罪己之盛心也。凡我臣工，又孰敢不祗承德意，而修其職分之所未盡者乎？臣固知北虜之不足平也。
伏讀聖制之篇終，有曰：「帝王之政，守在四夷。今朕欲求久安長治之術，無出于守之一端。欲得其守之之道，當何施用以盡其長且久焉？」且誡臣等毋忌毋隱，各著于篇。臣雖不肖，亦不敢上
translation_en:
…Your Majesty, endowed with sagely and divine qualities and both civil and martial accomplishments, has brought about harmonious and enduring government for twenty-three years now. Thus, wherever your virtue reaches, it nourishes like rain and dew; wherever your might reaches, it shakes like thunder; wherever your government reaches, it embraces and protects like Heaven and Earth. Its effects extend far beyond the tribute of hounds from Xilü and the offering of pheasants from Yuechang. Recently, the surviving remnants of the northern barbarians forgot our sovereign’s benevolence, which shelters them like Heaven, and gathered in raiding bands to invade, ravaging our people of Heaven, just as the imperial composition states. This is indeed the fault of civil and military officials who have failed to carry out their duties fully. If each fulfilled his office and exercised his abilities, the civilizing influence of the dance with shields and plumes would suffice to win over their wavering and disloyal hearts, while victorious strategies devised at court would break their arrogant and fierce spirit. They would then readily submit when conciliated and readily yield when attacked. Yet Your Majesty now says: “I have established no foundation of virtue within; therefore moral instruction cannot take effect without.” This truly expresses the noble spirit of Yu and Tang in laying blame upon themselves. Which of us officials would dare fail reverently to receive your virtuous intent and remedy whatever remains unfulfilled in his duties? Your servant is certain that the northern barbarians can readily be pacified.
I have reverently read these words at the close of the imperial composition: “In the government of emperors and kings, defense lies among the barbarians of the four quarters. Now I wish to seek a method of securing lasting peace and enduring order; nothing goes beyond this single matter of defense. To obtain the proper way of maintaining that defense, what measures should be employed to make its endurance and permanence complete?” You further admonish us servants to hold nothing back and conceal nothing, but each to set forth his views in writing. Though your servant is unworthy, I too dare not, toward my sovereign above…

title: 嘉靖二十三年進士登科錄
text:
負
天子下負所學而自棄于無諱之朝也竊以為
今日之計亦不能舍文武二者而別為之圖惟就
其壞于因循者而振揚之耳昔宋人西事之
興韓琦之陳謨也不急于其他而急于立紀
綱歐陽脩之陳謨也不急于其他而急于明
賞罰此皆振揚之說也方今縉紳之士以文
名者盖已充斥于中外矣然文藝徒工而經
濟之未閑其弊也虛介胄之士以武名者盖
已布列于遐邇矣然團練徒勤而擊刺之未
===
閑其弊也玩文恬武嬉其事適等而武備之
衰為尤甚今欲立明作之功濟惇大之體建
萬世久安長治之策安得不立紀綱明賞罰
從其壞于因循者而振揚之也臣敢冒昧悉
以邊事之弊者為
陛下陳之中國之禦戎地險以為坊頃自大寧既
棄而東北之藩籬以薄東勝不守而西北之
形勢以孤此地險之失據其弊一也中國之
禦戎人和以為本頃自大同倡亂而人懷判
渙之謀諸鎮觀望而軍無紀律之固此人和

translation_en:
…fail the Son of Heaven, fail the learning I have acquired, and thereby cast myself aside in a court where frank speech is unrestricted. I humbly believe that our plans today cannot dispense with civil and military affairs and seek some other course. We need only reinvigorate what has deteriorated through complacent adherence to routine. When hostilities arose on the Song dynasty’s western frontier, Han Qi, in presenting his counsel, gave priority above all else to establishing order and discipline; Ouyang Xiu, in presenting his counsel, gave priority above all else to making rewards and punishments clear. These were both proposals for reinvigoration.
At present, gentlemen of official standing renowned for their literary accomplishments already abound at court and throughout the provinces. Yet they are merely skilled in literary composition, without proficiency in statecraft: their failing is emptiness. Armored warriors renowned for martial prowess are already stationed far and near. Yet they are merely diligent in drilling their units, without proficiency in actual combat: their failing is laxity. Civil officials are complacent and military men idle; in this they are alike, but the decline in military preparedness is especially severe. If we now wish to achieve enlightened action, give effect to a substantial and broad foundation, and establish a policy securing lasting peace and enduring order for ten thousand generations, how can we avoid establishing order and discipline, making rewards and punishments clear, and reinvigorating what has deteriorated through complacent adherence to routine? Your servant ventures to lay before Your Majesty all the failings in frontier affairs.
In defending against the Rong, China relies on natural barriers as its bulwarks. Since Daning was abandoned, the defenses of the northeast have weakened; since Dongsheng was left undefended, the strategic position of the northwest has become isolated. This loss of control over natural barriers is the first failing. In defending against the Rong, China takes unity among its people as its foundation. Since Datong led the way in rebellion, men have harbored schemes of revolt and disunion; the various frontier garrisons have waited to see how events would unfold, and the armies have lacked firm discipline. This unity among the people…

title: 嘉靖二十三年進士登科錄
text:
之未至其弊二也中國之禦戎兵食以爲具
頃自屯政不脩而列屯無可仰之資鹽法未
清而轉漕無飛輓之助此兵食之未充其弊
三也弊端日新則邊備日隳而臣愚以爲非
一朝一夕之故也
陛下誠建久安長治之策以盡夫守之之道亦惟
察其致弊之原亟爲之所而已矣臣嘗妄論
今之事宜有六而攻討之術不與焉明居重
馭輕之權則畿兵之簡閱不可以不嚴也脩
列屯固圉之畧則土兵之團練不可以不恤
===
也廣推誠授任之道則精擇久任之說不可
以不行也慎招携懷遠之圖則撫綏節制之
宜不可以不詳也爲深根固本之慮則繭絲
保障之辨不可以不早也求足國裕用之規
則酌盈濟虛之道不可以不力也凡此數者
臣蓋日夜思之而未知其合于
國體否也今
陛下以天下爲度以生民爲念深求夫守之之道
則惟擇將擇相與之共理而已矣蓋將所以
捍衛于外相則計其功過詔王而馭之者也

punctuated:
之未至，其弊二也。中國之禦戎，兵食以爲具。頃自屯政不脩，而列屯無可仰之資；鹽法未清，而轉漕無飛輓之助。此兵食之未充，其弊三也。弊端日新，則邊備日隳，而臣愚以爲非一朝一夕之故也。
陛下誠建久安長治之策，以盡夫守之之道，亦惟察其致弊之原，亟爲之所而已矣。臣嘗妄論今之事宜有六，而攻討之術不與焉。明居重馭輕之權，則畿兵之簡閱不可以不嚴也；脩列屯固圉之畧，則土兵之團練不可以不恤也；廣推誠授任之道，則精擇久任之說不可以不行也；慎招携懷遠之圖，則撫綏節制之宜不可以不詳也；爲深根固本之慮，則繭絲保障之辨不可以不早也；求足國裕用之規，則酌盈濟虛之道不可以不力也。凡此數者，臣蓋日夜思之，而未知其合于國體否也。
今陛下以天下爲度，以生民爲念，深求夫守之之道，則惟擇將擇相，與之共理而已矣。蓋將所以捍衛于外，相則計其功過，詔王而馭之者也。
translation_en:
…has not been fully achieved: this is the second failing. In defending against the northern peoples, China relies on troops and provisions as its means. Of late, the administration of military agricultural colonies has fallen into disrepair, leaving the various colonies without resources on which to depend; the salt regulations have not been put in order, leaving grain transport without the assistance needed for swift delivery. This insufficiency of troops and provisions is the third failing. As fresh abuses arise daily, frontier defenses daily deteriorate. In my humble judgment, this state of affairs has not come about overnight.
If Your Majesty truly establishes a policy for enduring peace and lasting order, fully realizing the way of defense, what is needed is simply to examine the sources of these abuses and urgently take measures to address them. Your servant has ventured to argue that six measures are appropriate to present circumstances; methods of offensive warfare are not among them. To make clear the strategic principle of maintaining strength at the center to control the outlying regions, selection and inspection of the troops in the capital region must be rigorous. To improve the strategy of establishing garrisons to secure the borders, the organization and training of local troops must receive careful attention. To extend the practice of entrusting responsibilities with sincere confidence, the policy of choosing men carefully and retaining them long in office must be implemented. To proceed cautiously in winning over the estranged and cherishing those afar, the appropriate means of pacification and military command must be considered in detail. To plan for deep roots and a firm foundation, an early distinction must be drawn between extracting revenue—as one draws silk from cocoons—and safeguarding the people. To seek a plan that makes the state prosperous and provides ample resources, vigorous efforts must be made to draw upon surpluses to remedy shortages. Your servant has pondered all these matters day and night, yet does not know whether they accord with the proper ordering of the state.
Now Your Majesty takes all under Heaven as the scope of your concern, keeps the people's welfare in mind, and searches deeply for the way of defense. What is needed is simply to select generals and chief ministers and govern together with them. For generals defend the realm externally, while chief ministers assess their merits and faults, report to the sovereign, and exercise control over them.

title: 嘉靖二十三年進士登科錄
text:
昔漢高之王秦也有蕭何爲之謀而後韓信
得以畢其策宣帝之屯金城也有魏相爲之
主而後趙充國得以定其功唐宗之定蜀也
有杜黄裳爲之輔而後高崇文得以展其志
天下之事未有不由于君臣一德將相戮力
而可與有成者今從容密勿者有張仲之賢
寵握韜鈐者有吉甫之畧而又益求遺才搜
剔弊陋沉毅有斷而不重發以隳其功更張
有漸而不輕爲以速其敗則謀運于帷幄之
中而業彰于萬里之遠
===
大業之固當與天地同久而胡虜一時之驛騷旋
即底定矣又何足以勞
聖慮哉然臣于此復有獻焉昔孟軻氏有曰孰不
爲守守身守之本也是以古先哲王承曆數
之重爲華夷之主雖天下有一之不理皆爲
王政之缺而尤急于守身姦聲亂色足以蕩
吾守也則斥之淫樂慝禮足以移吾守也則
絶之便嬖側媚足以搖吾守也則遠之甘言
卑辭足以亂吾守也則放之雖在紛華波蕩
之中幽獨得肆之地而精之一之克之復之

卑辭足以亂吾守也則放之雖在紛華波蕩
之中幽獨得肆之地而精之一之克之復之
punctuated:
昔漢高之王秦也，有蕭何爲之謀，而後韓信得以畢其策；宣帝之屯金城也，有魏相爲之主，而後趙充國得以定其功；唐宗之定蜀也，有杜黄裳爲之輔，而後高崇文得以展其志。天下之事，未有不由于君臣一德、將相戮力而可與有成者。今從容密勿者有張仲之賢，寵握韜鈐者有吉甫之畧，而又益求遺才，搜剔弊陋，沉毅有斷，而不重發以隳其功；更張有漸，而不輕爲以速其敗，則謀運于帷幄之中，而業彰于萬里之遠。大業之固，當與天地同久，而胡虜一時之驛騷，旋即底定矣，又何足以勞聖慮哉？
然臣于此復有獻焉。昔孟軻氏有曰：「孰不爲守？守身，守之本也。」是以古先哲王承曆數之重，爲華夷之主，雖天下有一之不理，皆爲王政之缺，而尤急于守身。姦聲亂色足以蕩吾守也，則斥之；淫樂慝禮足以移吾守也，則絶之；便嬖側媚足以搖吾守也，則遠之；甘言卑辭足以亂吾守也，則放之。雖在紛華波蕩之中、幽獨得肆之地，而精之一之，克之復之。
translation_en:
When Gaozu of Han ruled Qin [?], only with Xiao He planning for him was Han Xin able to carry his strategy through. When Emperor Xuan stationed troops at Jincheng, only with Wei Xiang supporting the undertaking was Zhao Chongguo able to secure his achievement. When the Tang emperor pacified Shu, only with Du Huangshang assisting him was Gao Chongwen able to realize his ambition. No undertaking in the realm has ever succeeded without ruler and ministers being united in virtue, and generals and chief councilors joining their efforts. Today, those who deliberate calmly and diligently on confidential affairs possess the worthiness of Zhang Zhong, and those entrusted with military command [?] possess the strategic ability of Jifu. If, moreover, overlooked talent is sought still more diligently and abuses and shortcomings are ferreted out and removed; if resolve is firm and decisions decisive, without repeated mobilizations that undermine achievements; and if reforms proceed gradually, without rash action that hastens failure—then plans will be devised within the command tent, and achievements will shine forth ten thousand li away. The great imperial enterprise, firmly established, will endure as long as Heaven and Earth, while the passing disturbances caused by the northern barbarians will soon be quelled. How could these warrant troubling Your Majesty’s sagely thoughts?
Yet your servant has a further observation to offer. Meng Ke once said: “What is there that should not be guarded? Guarding oneself is the foundation of all guarding.” Thus the wise kings of antiquity bore the weighty charge of Heaven’s ordained succession and ruled over both the Chinese and the outer peoples. Although even a single matter left in disorder anywhere under Heaven constituted a defect in royal government, they gave particular urgency to guarding themselves. If depraved sounds and licentious sights could sweep away their self-command, they rejected them; if dissolute music and corrupt rites could displace it, they severed all connection with them; if intimate favorites and obsequious attendants could shake it, they kept them at a distance; and if sweet words and servile speech could disrupt it, they dismissed those who uttered them. Even amid the tumultuous allure of worldly splendor, or in secluded places where they could indulge themselves unchecked, they refined and unified their purpose, mastered themselves, and returned to proper conduct…

title: 嘉靖二十三年進士登科錄
text:
凜然如對神明不敢失守者誠以能守其身
則能守天下也我
皇祖之訓曰人心虛靈乘氣機出入操而存之爲
難所以光啓
一統之業而垂之萬世者盖本諸此今
陛下弘紹丕圖益敦
前烈
敬一有箴而操存于内者爲甚嚴五箴有註而省
察于外者爲甚密以此而取人則有克知灼
見之明而任賢勿貳矣以此而立政則有旋
===
乾轉坤之功而庶績咸熙矣是故其本在君
心其輔在將相其具在紀綱久安長治之策
在
陛下一加之意而已臣又何言哉臣愚不識忌諱
干冒
天威無任戰慄隕越之至臣謹對

在
陛下一加之意而已臣又何言哉臣愚不識忌諱
干冐
天威無任戰慄殞越之至臣謹對
punctuated: 凜然如對神明，不敢失守者，誠以能守其身，則能守天下也。我皇祖之訓曰：「人心虛靈，乘氣機出入，操而存之爲難。」所以光啓一統之業而垂之萬世者，盖本諸此。今陛下弘紹丕圖，益敦前烈。《敬一》有箴，而操存于内者爲甚嚴；五箴有註，而省察于外者爲甚密。以此而取人，則有克知灼見之明，而任賢勿貳矣；以此而立政，則有旋乾轉坤之功，而庶績咸熙矣。是故其本在君心，其輔在將相，其具在紀綱。久安長治之策，在陛下一加之意而已，臣又何言哉！臣愚，不識忌諱，干冒天威，無任戰慄隕越之至。臣謹對。
translation_en:
…standing in awe as though before divine spirits, never daring to let down their guard: this was truly because those who can guard their own persons can guard all under Heaven. Our imperial ancestor’s instruction states: “The human mind is empty and numinous; it comes and goes with the workings of vital energy. To hold fast to it and preserve it is difficult.” His glorious founding of a unified realm, handed down for ten thousand generations, was surely rooted in this.

Now Your Majesty carries forward the great imperial undertaking and further strengthens the achievements of your predecessors. You have composed the Admonition on Reverent Unity (Jingyi), exercising the utmost rigor in holding fast to and preserving the mind within; you have annotated the Five Admonitions, exercising the utmost care in examining outward conduct. If you select men on this basis, you will possess the discernment to know them truly and see them clearly, and will entrust responsibility to the worthy without hesitation. If you establish government on this basis, you will achieve the transformation of Heaven and Earth, and all undertakings will flourish.

Thus the foundation lies in the ruler’s mind, the assistance lies in his generals and chief ministers, and the instruments lie in the governing framework and discipline. The policy for lasting peace and enduring good government requires only that Your Majesty give this your attention. What more can your servant say? Your servant is foolish and ignorant of what must not be said, and has offended Your Heavenly Majesty. I am overwhelmed with trembling and dread. Your servant respectfully submits this reply.

臣吳情
臣對臣聞帝王之制馭遠夷也心不可一念
忘而其威則不可褻備不可一日弛而其用
則不可輕心不忘則本立本立而允塞之猷
基矣備不弛則政脩政脩而無競之烈著矣
夫允塞之猷日新之盛德也無競之烈富有
之大業也有盛德以來歸款之誠有大業以
折驕悍之氣所謂明王慎德四夷咸賓者而
又何憂於遠人之不服哉然而醜虜之性未
易憬悟向背之情尤為叵測吾惟心弗忘而
===
備弗弛於其來也則懲而禦之其去也則備
而守之以養吾威以制吾用斯則萬全之道
也苟慮之不審持之不固而徒與之爭勝負
于強弱之間則雖百戰百勝而幕南無王庭
酒泉列亭障猶為策之最下者豈帝王之所
當務哉故曰其政不在威強而在德業其具
不在兵食而在紀綱其本不在邊境而在朝
廷此則制馭萬全之常道而臣之所謂心不
可忘而備不可弛者誠亦有見于此也夫心
忘則備弛用輕則威褻故雖款塞稱臣不足

臣吳情。

臣對：臣聞帝王之制馭遠夷也，心不可一念忘，而其威則不可褻；備不可一日弛，而其用則不可輕。心不忘則本立，本立而允塞之猷基矣；備不弛則政脩，政脩而無競之烈著矣。夫允塞之猷，日新之盛德也；無競之烈，富有之大業也。有盛德以來歸款之誠，有大業以折驕悍之氣，所謂明王慎德，四夷咸賓者，而又何憂於遠人之不服哉？然而醜虜之性未易憬悟，向背之情尤為叵測。吾惟心弗忘而備弗弛，於其來也則懲而禦之，其去也則備而守之，以養吾威，以制吾用，斯則萬全之道也。苟慮之不審，持之不固，而徒與之爭勝負于強弱之間，則雖百戰百勝，而幕南無王庭，酒泉列亭障，猶為策之最下者，豈帝王之所當務哉？故曰：其政不在威強，而在德業；其具不在兵食，而在紀綱；其本不在邊境，而在朝廷。此則制馭萬全之常道，而臣之所謂心不可忘而備不可弛者，誠亦有見于此也。夫心忘則備弛，用輕則威褻，故雖款塞稱臣，不足
translation_en:
Your servant, Wu Qing.

Your servant replies: I have heard that, in emperors’ and kings’ control of distant foreign peoples, concern must not lapse for a single moment, yet their awe-inspiring power must not be debased; preparedness must not slacken for a single day, yet force must not be employed lightly. When concern does not lapse, the foundation is established; with the foundation established, plans grounded in sincerity and fullness take root. When preparedness does not slacken, government is well ordered; with government well ordered, unrivaled achievements become manifest. Such plans embody flourishing virtue renewed daily; such achievements constitute a great enterprise of abundant resources. With flourishing virtue to elicit sincere submission, and a great enterprise to break their arrogant and fierce spirit, this is what is meant by “The enlightened king attends carefully to his virtue, and the foreign peoples of the four quarters all come as guests.” Why, then, worry that distant peoples will not submit?

Yet the nature of these vile enemies is not easily brought to understanding, and their inclination toward allegiance or defection is especially unfathomable. We must simply never let our concern lapse or our preparedness slacken. When they come, we punish and repel them; when they withdraw, we maintain our preparations and defenses. In this way we nurture our awe-inspiring power and regulate our use of force: this is the way to complete security. If our deliberations are careless and our resolve unsteady, and we merely contend with them for victory through comparative strength, then even if we win every battle, leave no royal court south of the desert, and line Jiuquan with watch posts and frontier fortifications, this remains the lowest kind of strategy. How could this be what emperors and kings ought to pursue?

Thus I say: the governance required lies in virtue and achievement, rather than coercive might; its instruments lie in institutional order and discipline, rather than troops and provisions; its foundation lies in the imperial court, rather than the frontier. This is the enduring way to exercise control with complete security. My contention that concern must never lapse and preparedness must never slacken truly rests on this understanding. When concern lapses, preparedness slackens; when force is used lightly, awe-inspiring power is debased. Thus, even if they approach the frontier and declare themselves subjects, this is not sufficient …

title: 嘉靖二十三年進士登科錄
text:
爲喜恣肆侵掠不足爲怒而吾之所以自治
者惟備禦之有素是圖也
陛下不以經生卑臣而顧錫之以
清問寛之以毋忌諭之以毋隱而且以乆安長
治之道誘之使言臣雖卑之不敢高論而感
激思奮寧不有以一吐經生之常談哉蓋臣
自游學校常慨然有經營天下之志雖未敢
自附於孔明仲淹其人而於所謂内中國外
遠夷振紀綱脩德業而不可忘以弛者則嘗
區畫一二想望
===
明天子之廷而欲進其說乆矣第趙充國以漢之
老將猶謂兵難遥度而願至金城以圖方畧
矧經生以農之子跧伏民間不諳兵畧而徒
欲掇拾舊聞以塞
明詔則亦何足以仰副
陛下保衛生靈撫安夷夏之盛心也哉然而舍舊
所聞又無可以效芹曝之獻者是故有允文
允武之全德焉有無怠無荒之大猷焉有附
民而不毒民之仁焉有養兵而不窮兵之要
焉臣請爲

陛下不以經生卑臣，而顧錫之以清問，寛之以毋忌，諭之以毋隱，而且以乆安長治之道誘之使言。臣雖卑之不敢高論，而感激思奮，寧不有以一吐經生之常談哉？蓋臣自游學校，常慨然有經營天下之志，雖未敢自附於孔明、仲淹其人，而於所謂内中國、外遠夷，振紀綱、脩德業，而不可忘以弛者，則嘗區畫一二，想望明天子之廷而欲進其說乆矣。第趙充國以漢之老將，猶謂兵難遥度，而願至金城以圖方畧。矧經生以農之子，跧伏民間，不諳兵畧，而徒欲掇拾舊聞以塞明詔，則亦何足以仰副陛下保衛生靈、撫安夷夏之盛心也哉？然而舍舊所聞，又無可以效芹曝之獻者。是故有允文允武之全德焉，有無怠無荒之大猷焉，有附民而不毒民之仁焉，有養兵而不窮兵之要焉。臣請爲
translation_en:
…cause for joy, nor is their unbridled raiding and plundering sufficient cause for anger. In putting our own affairs in order, our sole concern should be to ensure that preparations for defense are well established.

Your Majesty has not looked down upon your servant as a mere student of the Classics, but has graciously bestowed searching questions upon me, allowed me to speak without apprehension, instructed me to conceal nothing, and further encouraged me to discuss the way to lasting peace and enduring good government. Though your servant is lowly [?] and dares not offer lofty discourse, gratitude moves me to exert myself: how could I fail to give voice, for once, to a classical student's commonplace views? Ever since I attended school, I have cherished an earnest ambition to bring order to the realm. Although I have never dared to rank myself with Kongming or Zhongyan, I have devised a few plans concerning what is called treating the central realm as the inner domain and distant foreign peoples as the outer domain, strengthening the governing order, and cultivating virtue and its works—matters that must never be forgotten or allowed to lapse. I have long gazed in hope toward the court of an enlightened Son of Heaven, wishing to present these views. Yet even Zhao Chongguo, a veteran general of the Han, said that military affairs were difficult to assess from afar and wished to go to Jincheng to devise a strategy. How much more does this apply to a student of the Classics, the son of a farmer, living obscurely among the common people and unfamiliar with military strategy! If I merely gather scraps of past learning to answer your enlightened edict, how could that possibly fulfill Your Majesty's noble desire to protect the people and bring peace to foreign peoples and the Chinese alike? Yet apart from what I have previously learned, I have nothing to offer as my humble gift of celery and warming sunshine. Thus there is the complete virtue of excellence in both civil and military affairs; there is the great plan of neither slackening nor indulging in excess; there is the benevolence that wins the people's allegiance without harming them; and there are the essentials of sustaining troops without exhausting them in warfare. Your servant begs to set these forth for…

title: 嘉靖二十三年進士登科錄
text:
陛下一陳之臣聞夷狄之患自古有之而苗民逆
命昆夷不殄雖以虞周之盛亦不能免也顧
其制馭之道一則儆戒無虞一則脩攘有要
使後世圖治之君願治之佐仰慕企望而不
可及此則虞周之所以爲盛也且虞帝不可
尚已姑自成周觀之天保以上治内而君臣
之德合采薇以下治外而夷夏之防嚴其所
以致是者盖曰緝熈敬止也曰於皇執競也
曰矢文德塞王猷也其脩之君者未嘗一念
忘也曰有嚴有翼也曰憂心悄悄也曰共武
===
服定王國也其脩之臣者未嘗一念忘也是
則其本既立而允塞之猷所由以基也其在
當時抑又兵師之制寓之井田無事則爲比
閭族黨州鄉之民而統于大司徒有事則爲
伍两卒旅軍師之衆而屬之大司馬鷹揚蹈
厲之將固不外於都俞揖遜之公卿也夫是
以兵農一致農聚而兵即存文武同方文敷
而武亦振以之守者此道也以之戰者亦此
道也與之守者此民也與之戰者亦此民也
自時厥後知此義者則鮮矣是故漢則困於

陛下一陳之。臣聞夷狄之患，自古有之，而苗民逆命，昆夷不殄，雖以虞周之盛，亦不能免也。顧其制馭之道，一則儆戒無虞，一則脩攘有要，使後世圖治之君、願治之佐，仰慕企望而不可及，此則虞周之所以爲盛也。且虞帝不可尚已，姑自成周觀之：《天保》以上治内，而君臣之德合；《采薇》以下治外，而夷夏之防嚴。其所以致是者，盖曰「緝熈敬止」也，曰「於皇執競」也，曰「矢文德，塞王猷」也，其脩之君者，未嘗一念忘也；曰「有嚴有翼」也，曰「憂心悄悄」也，曰「共武服，定王國」也，其脩之臣者，未嘗一念忘也。是則其本既立，而允塞之猷所由以基也。

其在當時，抑又兵師之制寓之井田，無事則爲比、閭、族、黨、州、鄉之民，而統于大司徒；有事則爲伍、两、卒、旅、軍、師之衆，而屬之大司馬。鷹揚蹈厲之將，固不外於都俞揖遜之公卿也。夫是以兵農一致，農聚而兵即存；文武同方，文敷而武亦振。以之守者，此道也；以之戰者，亦此道也。與之守者，此民也；與之戰者，亦此民也。自時厥後，知此義者則鮮矣。是故漢則困於
