…set these forth one by one for Your Majesty. Your servant has heard that troubles from the Yi and Di have existed since antiquity. The Miao people defied commands, and the Kunyi were not eradicated: even Yu and Zhou, in their flourishing days, could not escape such troubles. Yet their methods of controlling them consisted, on the one hand, in remaining vigilant when no danger threatened and, on the other, in attending to internal preparations and repelling external enemies according to essential principles. Rulers of later ages who sought good government, and ministers who desired it, looked up to them in admiration and aspiration but could not equal them. This is what made Yu and Zhou so flourishing. The emperor of Yu cannot be surpassed; let us therefore consider the established Zhou order. The poems through “Heaven Protects” (Tian bao) concern ordering internal affairs, so that the virtues of ruler and ministers were united; those from “Gathering Bracken” (Cai wei) onward concern ordering external affairs, so that the boundary between the Yi and the Xia was strictly maintained. What brought this about is expressed in the words “Continue in brightness and abide in reverence,” “Ah, august and steadfast in strength,” and “Display civil virtue and fulfill the king’s plans.” In cultivating these qualities, the ruler never forgot them for a single moment. It is also expressed in the words “Reverent and attentive,” “My anxious heart is deeply troubled,” and “Undertake martial service and secure the royal realm.” In cultivating these qualities, the ministers never forgot them for a single moment. Thus the root was established, providing the foundation for truly substantial plans.

At that time, moreover, military organization was embedded in the well-field system. In times of peace, the people belonged to neighborhood groups (bi), hamlets (lü), clans (zu), communities (dang), districts (zhou), and townships (xiang), under the Minister of Education. When military affairs arose, they formed squads (wu), platoons (liang), companies (zu), battalions (lü), armies (jun), and divisions (shi), under the Minister of War. Generals who soared like hawks and advanced with martial vigor were none other than the dukes and ministers who exchanged assent in council and observed courteous deference. Thus soldiers and farmers formed a single body: wherever farmers gathered, soldiers were already present. Civil and military affairs followed the same course: as civil governance spread, military strength also flourished. This was the way employed in defense, and the same way was employed in battle. These were the people with whom one defended, and these same people were those with whom one fought. From that time onward, few understood this principle. Thus the Han was hard pressed by …

之晦塞矣惟我
太祖高皇帝繼天立極驅之於沙漠之外而復帝
王所自立之中國可謂有功於天地有功於
生民是雖延之億萬年而天地之所以報其
功德者固爲無疆也况天下既定務脩文德
以開太平此即周武王下車而訪範敘疇聿

===
祖訓懋脩
文德天下乂安至我
陛下以大有爲之聖益起而覲揚之明作以勵治
功敦大以裕治體文武並用恩威並伸所謂
天下有道守在四夷者固将與天地相爲悠
久也夫何比年以来北虜入寇竊伺我藩籬
虔劉我邊庶未免厪我
皇上宵旰之隱憂臣知
陛下之心固未嘗一日忘乎邊境矣而邊境之将

匈奴，唐則衰於藩鎮，宋則削於契丹。迨至胡元入主中國，則三綱淪、九法斁，而天地且爲之晦塞矣。惟我太祖高皇帝繼天立極，驅之於沙漠之外，而復帝王所自立之中國，可謂有功於天地，有功於生民。是雖延之億萬年，而天地之所以報其功德者，固爲無疆也。况天下既定，務脩文德，以開太平，此即周武王下車而訪範敘疇，聿求懿德，以肆于時夏之心也。
列聖相承，光昭祖訓，懋脩文德，天下乂安。至我陛下，以大有爲之聖，益起而覲揚之，明作以勵治功，敦大以裕治體，文武並用，恩威並伸。所謂天下有道，守在四夷者，固将與天地相爲悠久也。夫何比年以来，北虜入寇，竊伺我藩籬，虔劉我邊庶，未免厪我皇上宵旰之隱憂？臣知陛下之心，固未嘗一日忘乎邊境矣。而邊境之将領，能無紈袴不知兵、徒讀父書之流矣乎？邊
translation_en:
…the Xiongnu; the Tang declined because of the regional military commands, and the Song was diminished by the Khitan. When the foreign Yuan came to rule China, the Three Bonds fell into ruin and the nine fundamental principles of government were corrupted, so that even Heaven and Earth were darkened and obstructed. Our Emperor Taizu Gao alone succeeded to Heaven’s mandate and established the supreme standard, driving them beyond the desert and restoring the China in which the ancient emperors and kings had established themselves. Truly, he rendered service to Heaven and Earth and to the people. Even over hundreds of millions of years, Heaven and Earth’s recompense for his achievements and virtue will assuredly know no bounds. Moreover, once the realm was pacified, he devoted himself to cultivating civil virtue and opening an age of great peace. This was precisely the spirit of King Wu of Zhou, who, upon descending from his chariot, sought instruction in the Great Plan and the ordering of its nine categories, seeking excellent virtue to spread throughout this land of Xia.
Successive sage sovereigns made the ancestral instructions shine forth and diligently cultivated civil virtue, bringing order and peace to the realm. Now Your Majesty, a sage capable of great achievements, has further arisen to manifest and exalt this legacy. Through enlightened action you spur the accomplishments of government; through generosity and breadth you enrich its foundations. Civil and military means are employed together, and both benevolence and authority are extended. This is what is meant by the saying, “When the realm possesses the Way, its defense lies among the peoples of the four quarters.” Surely this state of affairs should endure as long as Heaven and Earth. Why, then, in recent years have the northern barbarians invaded, stealthily watching for openings in our defenses and slaughtering our frontier people, inevitably burdening our Emperor with anxious concern from before dawn until late at night? Your servant knows that Your Majesty has never for a single day forgotten the frontier. Yet among the frontier commanders, can there be none of those pampered sons of privilege who know nothing of warfare, who merely read their fathers’ military books? At the frontier…

title: 嘉靖二十三年進士登科錄
text:
境之卒戍能無朽戈敝甲失伍離次而無鬪
志者乎邊境之撫巡能無徒握重權而未知
歌咏勞苦之典激勵作興之道者乎此無競
之烈所繇以弗著也而
陛下策臣乃引之以自責曰此固朕以罔德基之
立于中是以教化莫克行于外臣有以仰窺
陛下制治未亂保邦未危之心不能以一日遑暇
是以不自知其謙冲至此也
陛下此心真所謂不出戶庭之間而可以折衝千
里之外干羽之舞文教之脩率是道也詩云
===
勉勉我王綱紀四方
陛下實有之是故虜之入寇雖若可憂而
陛下赫業之
天威臣工蚤夜之振勵固足以寒氈裘之膽而折
其心此兵家所謂先聲也雖然不足憂之中
而深可憂者實在焉何也向背靡常者醜虜
之情也是故聖王之於夷狄毎治之以不治
不以其來而懾不以其去而弛也是以不憂
外患之未息而深憂內治之未脩不以裔夷
之单弱為可喜而恒以吾之備禦之素定為

translation_en:
…among the soldiers garrisoning the frontier, can there be none with rotten spear shafts and worn-out armor, who abandon their ranks and posts and have no will to fight? Among the frontier grand coordinators and regional inspectors, can there be none who merely wield great authority without understanding the established practice of celebrating the soldiers’ hardships in song, or the means of encouraging and rousing them? This is why achievements of unrivaled might have failed to become manifest. Yet in putting your policy question to your servant, Your Majesty takes this upon yourself as grounds for self-reproach, saying: “This surely arises because I, lacking virtue, have established its foundation within; thus moral instruction cannot take effect beyond.” Your servant can thereby glimpse Your Majesty’s determination to secure order before disorder arises and safeguard the realm before danger comes—a concern that allows you not a single day of leisure. Thus, without realizing it, you have carried your humility to this degree.

This intention of Your Majesty’s truly exemplifies what is meant by overcoming an enemy a thousand li away without stepping beyond one’s doors and courtyard. The dance with shields and feathers and the cultivation of civil instruction both follow this way. The Book of Odes says: “Diligent is our king, bringing order to the four quarters.” Your Majesty truly possesses this quality. Thus, although the incursions of the northern foes may seem cause for concern, Your Majesty’s awesome [?] heavenly majesty and your officials’ strenuous efforts morning and night are surely sufficient to chill the courage of these felt-clad men and break their resolve. This is what military strategists call establishing one’s prestige in advance.

Nevertheless, within what seems no cause for concern there is indeed something deeply concerning. Why? These vile foes are by nature inconstant in their allegiance and hostility. Hence, in dealing with the peoples beyond the borders, sage kings have always governed them through noninterference: neither intimidated by their coming nor lax upon their departure. They therefore worry less that external troubles have not ceased than that internal government remains uncultivated. They take no delight in the weakness of distant foreign peoples, but always regard the prior establishment of our own defensive preparations as…

title: 嘉靖二十三年進士登科錄
text:
無患也然則所以張皇六師克詰戎兵者豈
無道哉是宜慎之紀綱明賞罰之權核功罪
之當使太阿之柄常在
朝廷可也若希冀無事因循除拜如魏博之姑
息不可也若誅求責望損威傷重如承倩之
將命不可也若優游牽制而啓王武俊之邪
謀不可也若隔絕排擯而致李懷光之怨望
不可也務使有紀律之嚴無壅蔽之患則雖
無救於既往尚可責效於將來行之既久臣
見將領之在邊境也賞既酬勞恩常踰望推
===
心置腹效死恐後矣卒戍之在邊境也沙草
晨牧河氷夜渡風雨罷勞饑渴不困矣不必
司馬孫吳頗牧之復出而
陛下未嘗無將也不必采薇出車六月之師之復
興而
陛下未嘗無兵也是故據鞍矍鑠者可遣也不親
戎服輕裘緩帶者亦可遣也膂力方剛者可
遣也身不跨馬射不穿札者亦可遣也閑之
以節制則能使之有勇附之以仁義則能使
之知方由是畜芻糧備器械謹斥堠嚴瞭望

punctuated: 無患也。然則所以張皇六師、克詰戎兵者，豈無道哉？是宜慎之紀綱，明賞罰之權，核功罪之當，使太阿之柄常在朝廷可也。若希冀無事，因循除拜，如魏博之姑息，不可也；若誅求責望，損威傷重，如承倩之將命，不可也；若優游牽制，而啓王武俊之邪謀，不可也；若隔絕排擯，而致李懷光之怨望，不可也。務使有紀律之嚴，無壅蔽之患，則雖無救於既往，尚可責效於將來。行之既久，臣見將領之在邊境也，賞既酬勞，恩常踰望，推心置腹，效死恐後矣；卒戍之在邊境也，沙草晨牧，河氷夜渡，風雨罷勞，饑渴不困矣。不必司馬、孫吳、頗牧之復出，而陛下未嘗無將也；不必《采薇》《出車》《六月》之師之復興，而陛下未嘗無兵也。是故據鞍矍鑠者可遣也，不親戎服、輕裘緩帶者亦可遣也；膂力方剛者可遣也，身不跨馬、射不穿札者亦可遣也。閑之以節制，則能使之有勇；附之以仁義，則能使之知方。由是畜芻糧，備器械，謹斥堠，嚴瞭望。
translation_en:
…to be free from danger. Is there, then, no proper way to strengthen the Six Armies and put military forces in good order? One should carefully maintain their governing discipline [?], make clear the authority to reward and punish, and assess merits and offenses justly, so that the hilt of the sword Tai’a—the power of command—always remains with the court. It is unacceptable to hope that nothing will happen and make appointments by following established practice without reflection, as in the indulgence shown to Weibo. It is unacceptable to make oppressive demands and exact compliance, diminishing authority and impairing dignity, as when Chengqian carried out his mission. It is unacceptable to temporize and impose restraints in ways that encourage treacherous schemes like those of Wang Wujun. It is unacceptable to isolate and exclude men, provoking resentment like that of Li Huaiguang. Strive to ensure strict discipline and prevent the obstruction of information. Then, although past failures cannot be remedied, results may still be demanded in the future.

Once these measures have long been practiced, your servant foresees that commanders on the frontier, their service duly rewarded and imperial favor continually exceeding their expectations, will give their wholehearted trust and vie to be first to serve unto death. Soldiers garrisoning the frontier will pasture their horses among the sandy grasses at dawn and cross frozen rivers at night; amid wind, rain, and exhausting toil, hunger and thirst will not overcome them. Your Majesty need not await the return of Sima Rangju, Sun Wu, Wu Qi, Lian Po, and Li Mu to have commanders. Nor need Your Majesty await the revival of the armies celebrated in Gathering Bracken (Cai wei), Bringing Out the Chariots (Chu che), and The Sixth Month (Liu yue) to have troops.

Thus, men still hale and vigorous in the saddle may be dispatched, but so too may those who wear no military dress, clad instead in light furs with loosely fastened belts. Men in the prime of their physical strength may be dispatched, but so too may those who do not mount horses and whose arrows cannot pierce armor. Train them through military discipline, and they can be made courageous; bind them to you through benevolence and righteousness, and they can be made to understand proper conduct. On this basis, stockpile fodder and grain, prepare weapons and equipment, exercise care in scouting, and maintain strict watch…

title: 嘉靖二十三年進士登科錄
text:
當虜之来也而不畏其来吾惟堅壁清野而
不為結怨深讐之舉虜雖去也而猶若未去
吾惟日相警戒而恒有不測不克之嚴則以
飽待饑以逸待勞無戰之名有勝之實北虜
不足攘中國不足安而可保億萬年無事者
端在於此臣將歌匡王國佐天子之詩以為
國家頌
陛下北顧之憂不亦可盡舒也哉然臣又有說焉
荆楚之来王商宗濯濯之靈振矣然不敢怠
遑實基之也南北之蕩平周天子中興之功
偉矣然夙夜基命實致之也大雅抑之詩有
曰夙興夜寐灑掃庭內維民之章又曰脩爾
車馬弓矢戎兵用戒戎作用逖蠻方蓋內自
庭除之近外及蠻方之逺細而寢興灑掃之
常大而車馬戎兵之變慮無不周備無不飭
可謂勤矣然其用功切要之處則有曰視爾
友君子輯柔爾顏又曰相在爾室尚不愧于
屋陋此正子思所謂慎獨者而天德所自立
王道所從出也以
陛下文武神聖之資剛健中正之德並殷周之治

punctuated:
當虜之来也，而不畏其来，吾惟堅壁清野，而不為結怨深讐之舉。虜雖去也，而猶若未去，吾惟日相警戒，而恒有不測不克之嚴。則以飽待饑，以逸待勞，無戰之名，有勝之實。北虜不足攘，中國不足安，而可保億萬年無事者，端在於此。臣將歌「匡王國，佐天子」之詩，以為國家頌。陛下北顧之憂，不亦可盡舒也哉！
然臣又有說焉。荆楚之来王，商宗濯濯之靈振矣，然不敢怠遑，實基之也。南北之蕩平，周天子中興之功偉矣，然夙夜基命，實致之也。《大雅》〈抑〉之詩有曰：「夙興夜寐，灑掃庭內，維民之章。」又曰：「脩爾車馬，弓矢戎兵，用戒戎作，用逖蠻方。」蓋內自庭除之近，外及蠻方之逺，細而寢興灑掃之常，大而車馬戎兵之變，慮無不周，備無不飭，可謂勤矣。然其用功切要之處，則有曰：「視爾友君子，輯柔爾顏。」又曰：「相在爾室，尚不愧于屋陋。」此正子思所謂慎獨者，而天德所自立、王道所從出也。以陛下文武神聖之資，剛健中正之德，並殷周之治
translation_en:
When the barbarians come, we should not fear their coming. We need only strengthen our fortifications and clear the countryside of supplies, undertaking nothing that would create resentment and deepen enmity. Even after the barbarians have withdrawn, we should act as though they had not yet gone, warning one another daily and maintaining strict vigilance against the unexpected and the possibility of defeat. Thus, well fed, we await the hungry; rested, we await the weary. Without the name of having fought, we gain the substance of victory. The northern barbarians are not worth repelling, and the central realm is not worth securing [?]; yet the means of ensuring freedom from trouble for countless ages lies precisely here. Your servant will sing the poem that says, “Set the royal realm aright; assist the Son of Heaven,” as a hymn of praise to the state. Might not Your Majesty’s anxiety as you look north then be entirely relieved?
Yet your servant has something further to say. When Jing and Chu came to acknowledge royal authority, the resplendent spiritual might of the Shang ancestral sovereign was made manifest; yet its true foundation was his not daring to idle or take his ease. When north and south were pacified, great was the achievement of the Zhou Son of Heaven in restoring his dynasty; yet it was his laboring morning and night to establish the Mandate that truly brought this about. The poem “Admonition” (Yi) in the “Greater Odes” says: “Rise early and retire late; sprinkle and sweep within your courtyard, serving as a model for the people.” It also says: “Put your chariots and horses in order, your bows, arrows, and weapons of war, to guard against the outbreak of hostilities and keep the barbarian regions at a distance.” Thus, from the nearby courtyard within to the distant barbarian regions without, from such small daily matters as sleeping, rising, sprinkling, and sweeping to the great emergencies requiring chariots, horses, and weapons, no consideration is incomplete and no preparation left unattended. This may indeed be called diligence. Yet concerning the crucial point at which effort must be applied, the poem says: “When you look upon your friends, the noble men, make your countenance gentle and mild.” It also says: “Look to yourself within your chamber; may you have nothing to be ashamed of even in the secluded recesses of your house [?].” This is precisely what Zisi called “being watchful over oneself when alone”: it is the foundation of heavenly virtue and the source of the kingly Way. With Your Majesty’s natural gifts of civil and martial accomplishment, divine wisdom and sageliness, and your virtues of strength, vigor, centrality, and rectitude, to equal the good government of Yin and Zhou…

title: 嘉靖二十三年進士登科錄
text:
而遠軼帝王之盛誠無難者而臣惓惓一念
尤望
陛下自謹獨始則瑟兮僩兮赫兮喧兮而馴至於
光被四表格于上下雖中和位育之極亦可
坐而致也憬彼北虜將允喙奔突之不暇矣
而奚足累
光裕之
大烈也哉臣俯伏
闕廷牽制文義誠未能切磋究之以答稱
陛下之德意然使臣不以聖賢大學之道進而竊
===

punctuated: 而遠軼帝王之盛，誠無難者。而臣惓惓一念，尤望陛下自謹獨始，則瑟兮僩兮，赫兮喧兮，而馴至於光被四表，格于上下。雖中和位育之極，亦可坐而致也。憬彼北虜，將允喙奔突之不暇矣，而奚足累光裕之大烈也哉！臣俯伏闕廷，牽制文義，誠未能切磋究之，以答稱陛下之德意。然使臣不以聖賢大學之道進，而竊取五餌三表之餘，試以縛單于之頸、扼中行說之吭而撫其背之說，以瀆陛下，則洛陽少年之所以見黜于漢文者也，而臣豈敢哉！臣不勝隕越戰慄之至，臣謹對。
translation_en:
…and far surpass the flourishing rule of the ancient emperors and kings: this would indeed present no difficulty. Yet your servant’s most earnest wish is that Your Majesty begin by exercising vigilance when alone. Then, solemn and dignified, illustrious and majestic, you will gradually attain a state in which your radiance reaches the four quarters and extends to heaven above and earth below. Even the ultimate achievement of equilibrium and harmony, whereby heaven and earth take their proper places and all things are nourished, can be attained with ease. Those distant northern barbarians will have scarcely time to gasp and flee [?]; how could they possibly impair the great achievements of your glorious and abundant rule?

Your servant lies prostrate at the palace court. Constrained by the wording and meaning of the texts, I have truly been unable to examine and investigate these matters thoroughly enough to respond adequately to Your Majesty’s virtuous intentions. Yet if, instead of presenting the Way of the sages and worthies taught in the Great Learning, I were to borrow remnants of the schemes of the “five baits” and “three demonstrations,” venturing to profane Your Majesty’s hearing with proposals to bind the chanyu by the neck, seize Zhonghang Yue by the throat, and pat his back, this would be precisely what caused the young man of Luoyang to be rejected by Emperor Wen of the Han. How could your servant dare to do so? Overwhelmed by fear of falling short and trembling with apprehension, your servant respectfully submits this reply.
